cards.title: What Is Machine Learning?
cards.hook: Instead of hand-coding rules, you show a program examples and let it find the patterns — then it handles inputs it has never seen.

cards.title: The Perceptron
cards.hook: The 1958 perceptron was the first algorithm that learned its own weights from examples — the seed of everything, and the model whose limits sparked the first AI winter.

cards.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning
cards.hook: Do your examples come with answer keys? That one question splits machine learning into two very different jobs.

cards.title: Zer0Fit: Zero-Shot Tabular ML and Forecasting, Callable by Any LLM
cards.hook: Instead of training a model on your spreadsheet, an agent can now just ask a foundation model to guess — and get scores close to a tuned one, no training loop involved.

cards.title: Loss Functions
cards.hook: A loss function turns 'how wrong was I?' into a single number the model chases downhill — and the loss you pick decides what it learns to care about.

cards.title: How Neural Networks Learn: Backpropagation
cards.hook: A neural net learns by asking, for every weight, 'how much did you contribute to my mistake?' Backprop answers all of them at once.

cards.title: Gradient Descent
cards.hook: Lost in fog on a hillside, you'd feel for the steepest downhill step and take it, again and again. That's how models learn.

cards.title: Learning Rate & Schedules
cards.hook: The single most important hyperparameter: set it too high and training diverges, too low and it crawls — so we warm it up, then decay it.

cards.title: Learning Words Like a Child
cards.hook: Most models learn from data shuffled and replayed for hundreds of epochs. BabyCL learns word-object links from a child's-eye video in one pass through time — close to how a kid actually learns.

cards.title: Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors
cards.hook: The 1986 paper that made deep learning possible: run the error backward through the network with the chain rule, and you get every weight's gradient in one sweep.

cards.title: Predictive Coding as a Backprop Alternative (Deepity)
cards.hook: Backprop isn't the only way to assign credit in a neural net. A hobby C++ library reports predictive coding matching it on MNIST — once you make the slow part fast.

cards.title: Overfitting & Regularization
cards.hook: A model that aces its training data but flops on anything new hasn't learned — it has memorized. Regularization is the cure.

cards.title: The Illusion of Robustness: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Prediction Flips
cards.hook: A model's accuracy barely budges when you paste in random gibberish — but under the hood, a chunk of its individual answers silently flip, some right to wrong, some wrong to right.

cards.title: Beyond IID: How General Are Tabular Foundation Models, Really?
cards.hook: Tabular foundation models look great on standard IID benchmarks — but on temporal, grouped, high-dimensional, and non-IID data, plain tree-based models still win.

cards.title: Deep Double Descent
cards.hook: Bigger models should overfit, then get worse — right? Instead test error often dips, climbs, then dips again as model size grows, breaking the classic bias-variance story.

cards.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
cards.hook: You can prune over 90% of a trained network and keep its accuracy. The catch: a tiny 'winning ticket' subnetwork was hiding inside the dense one from the start.

cards.title: The Bias–Variance Tradeoff
cards.hook: Too simple and your model misses the pattern; too flexible and it chases noise. Generalization lives between the two.

cards.title: When Your Top Feature Makes Predictions Worse
cards.hook: A feature can top your model's importance ranking and still hurt accuracy. The only way to be sure it helps: delete it, retrain, and compare on held-out data.

cards.title: Grokking: Generalization Long After Overfitting
cards.hook: A network memorizes the training set and seems done. Keep training anyway, and much later it can suddenly snap into real generalization — an effect called grokking.

cards.title: Requential Coding: Pushing the Limits of Model Compression with Self-Generated Training Data
cards.hook: Bigger models are supposed to be harder to bound. This compressor only pays bits where a model's predictions disagree with a teacher — and the resulting bound gets TIGHTER as scale grows.

cards.title: Canalization Before Generalization: Grokking as a Dynamical Probe
cards.hook: Nudge weight decay briefly during grokking's plateau and you shift when generalization arrives. Early nudges scatter; later ones line up by dose — a hidden selection finishing unseen.

cards.title: Which Tasks Do Transformers Extrapolate To? Now Decidable
cards.hook: Transformers sometimes handle sequences longer than they trained on, sometimes not. For regular languages there's now a complete characterization — and a polynomial-time algorithm to check.

cards.title: Geometric Causal Models
cards.hook: Causal inference usually assumes i.i.d. data. This framework builds causal models around the symmetries data actually has — spatial, network, genomic — unlocking inference where classical methods don't apply.

cards.title: Train / Validation / Test Splits
cards.hook: If you tune and grade on the same data, you'll fool yourself. Keep a test set you never touch until the very end.

cards.title: A Randomized Trial on ChatGPT in the Classroom
cards.hook: Most claims about AI and student learning come from anecdote. OpenAI ran the other kind of study: over 1,000 students, randomized, on a real university assignment.

cards.title: The One-Word Census: Answer-Choice Conformity Across 44 Language Models
cards.hook: Ask 44 different LLMs to name any word, no multiple choice — and 41% of them say 'serendipity.' A minimal new instrument measures just how herd-like models really are.

cards.title: Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the Human Quality of Voice AI
cards.hook: Voice AI benchmarks mostly grade transcripts. Hume AI's new eval says most systems still miss tone, hesitation, and emotion - the parts that make speech sound human.

cards.title: When a Model Says 90%, Does It Mean It?
cards.hook: Across 30 models, the confidence an LLM reports in words is only loosely coupled to the confidence in its logits — a lossy channel, not a readout.

cards.title: VGI-Bench: Can Video Models Reason by Generating?
cards.hook: Video generators appear to do zero-shot visual reasoning in their frames. Held to a benchmark that demands a valid evolving process, the best model — Seedance 2.0 — scores 51%.

cards.title: Anchoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
cards.hook: Show an LLM judge a previous score as mere context metadata and its rating drifts toward that number. Judgments you assumed were independent are quietly anchored to each other.

cards.title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion
cards.hook: Best agent configuration finished 20 of 97 real scientific workflows. And among failing Claude Code runs, 75.5% still signed off claiming they were done.

cards.title: Skill Issue: Are Skills Language-Invariant in LLMs?
cards.hook: Have a model play a game against itself, one copy in English and one in another language. Same model, same rules, same board — and markedly different playing strength.

cards.title: SWE Refactor Bench: Agents Can't Finish Migrations
cards.hook: Ask a coding agent to migrate a whole repo and it may just copy the old implementation to make tests pass. Audit for that, and only 5.4% of 520 runs survive.

cards.title: SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?
cards.hook: When software is part of the scientific instrument, a bad patch corrupts the evidence. The best agent tested clears under 50% of these repo-level scientific fixes.

cards.title: LLM Judges Can't Separate Trust from Truth
cards.hook: Ask a judge model for a trust score and a correctness verdict and you get two numbers — but they're not two pieces of evidence. Change the source label and both move.

cards.title: What 2,226 Reproduced ICML Papers Revealed
cards.hook: A community hackathon re-ran a third of ICML 2026. Half the papers had a claim verified — and 23% had a claim falsified or contested.

cards.title: How Rhetoric Reward-Hacks an AI Reviewer
cards.hook: Rewrite a paper's framing without changing a single result, and LLM reviewers move their scores. The effect is structured: evidence framing and novelty stance move them most.

cards.title: Who Thinks Best Depends on How Long You Let Them
cards.hook: Change the token budget and the leaderboard changes with it. Model rankings reversed on every benchmark tested — which means a single-budget eval is measuring the budget as much as the model.

cards.title: SWE-Bench ProMax: Refactoring as the Harder Coding Test
cards.hook: Coding benchmarks keep saturating and keep turning out to be broken. ProMax swaps bug-fixing for multi-file refactoring — and the best frontier model still only solves 41.2%.

cards.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability?
cards.hook: An agent score only means something if the task still requires the skill it claims to test. Auditing 2,385 traces, two-thirds showed the agent taking a shortcut instead.

cards.title: AI Tutors Jump In Too Soon
cards.hook: Put an LLM in the tutor's seat and it interrupts sooner and more often than a human would — and hands over the whole solution where a person would have offered a hint.

cards.title: LLMs Get Lost When Intent Keeps Moving
cards.hook: Real users don't state what they want up front — they reveal, revise, and redirect it mid-conversation. Rewrite existing benchmarks that way and scores drop across every model family.

cards.title: DynamicRubric: Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies
cards.hook: As a model improves, its candidate answers get so close in quality that the reward model can't tell them apart. DynamicRubric fixes the bottleneck by evolving the evaluator alongside the policy.

cards.title: An Exam for Active Observers
cards.hook: Human vision is a loop — look, form a hypothesis, look again. A new benchmark for that loop leaves frontier MLLMs scoring single digits, while humans average 96%.

cards.title: Hindcast: Replaying Prediction Markets to Evaluate LLM Forecasters
cards.hook: Backtesting an LLM forecaster on past events mostly measures its memory, not its foresight — because it can retrieve after-the-fact reports or was simply trained on data closer to the event.

cards.title: A Benchmark for Open-Ended Multi-Agent Coordination
cards.hook: 13 LLMs try to explore, trade, craft, and build together in an open world — and most manage only ~6% of normalized return. Communication, not raw capability, turns out to be the biggest lever.

cards.title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench: Testing the Limits of Agents on Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks
cards.hook: 46 terminal tasks that take hours, not minutes — and today's best agent still only nails 15% of them, with the average model managing barely 4%.

cards.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
cards.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

cards.title: Beyond IID: How General Are Tabular Foundation Models, Really?
cards.hook: Tabular foundation models look great on standard IID benchmarks — but on temporal, grouped, high-dimensional, and non-IID data, plain tree-based models still win.

cards.title: OSWorld 2.0: Long-Horizon Computer Use, Stress-Tested
cards.hook: 108 realistic computer-use workflows averaging 1.6 human-hours each expose how far agents are from professional-grade computer use — the best model completes only 20.6%.

cards.title: Beyond Static Leaderboards for Agents
cards.hook: Topping an agent leaderboard doesn't mean it'll work when deployed: aggregate-score rankings don't transfer out-of-distribution. Rank by predictive validity instead.

cards.title: Precision, Recall & F1
cards.hook: On rare events, a model can be 99% accurate and still useless. Precision and recall reveal what accuracy hides.

cards.title: Ignorance or Incompetence? Building Agent Tasks That Tell the Difference
cards.hook: When an agent fails a professional task, was it incapable or just missing a convention nobody published? This protocol splits the instruction from the private knowledge so you can test which.

cards.title: Paint What You See: A Benchmark for Dexterous Visual Tool Use
cards.hook: Ask a multimodal agent to repaint a reference image stroke by stroke and it stalls at roughly half-right — then gets worse the longer it works.

cards.title: Proper Scoring Rules Are Not Interchangeable as Training Objectives
cards.hook: Five scoring rules that all reward honest probabilities in theory produced five differently-behaved forecasters in practice — same accuracy, different shape of error.

cards.title: MobilePA-Bench: Phone Agents in a Live Sandbox
cards.hook: GUI benchmarks test tapping; function-call benchmarks test string matching. This one runs a real phone sandbox with live app databases — and frontier models get brittle fast.

cards.title: Visual Scaffolds Reveal What VLM Benchmarks Measure
cards.hook: Redraw the same spatial puzzle to make its structure legible and accuracy jumps up to 34 points — so was the benchmark ever testing reasoning?

cards.title: Forecast Collapse in Time-Series Foundation Models
cards.hook: Ask a forecasting model to predict hourly stock returns and it hedges into a nearly flat line — technically well-calibrated, useless for ranking. Per-series metrics never show you this.

cards.title: Knowing When to Stop: Adaptive Sampling for LLM Evals
cards.hook: Most evals run every item the same number of times, long after the estimate has stopped moving. Treat it as sequential measurement instead and 57–97% of those trials turn out to be unnecessary.

cards.title: Can LLM Agents Stick to the Script? A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Consistency in Interactive Narratives
cards.hook: Fluent writing is not the same as staying consistent: the best model keeps its story straight for only 42% of runs past 20 turns of adversarial play.

cards.title: Models Can Pass the Exam Without Knowing the Syllabus
cards.hook: Educational benchmarks test whether a model answers school questions. This one tests whether it knows which concept comes before which — and the best model scores 57%.

cards.title: DocOps: Benchmarking Agents That Edit Real Documents
cards.hook: Even frontier agents can't reliably edit complex documents: a verifiable benchmark pins the failures on three modes — state-tracking collapse, shallow verification, and destructive metadata edits.

cards.title: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation
cards.hook: Most agent-optimization papers report a one-shot gain and stop. Rerun the optimizer on new tasks and two of three popular methods actually make the agent worse than doing nothing.

cards.title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
cards.hook: IRT ranks models off a handful of items instead of averaging accuracy — but the math was built for human test-takers, and AI benchmarks break its assumptions in ways that quietly distort rankings.

cards.title: AdvancedMathBench: A Benchmark Suite for Advanced Mathematical Proof Generation and Verification
cards.hook: Frontier models look near-perfect on final-answer math benchmarks. Ask for a rigorous PhD-level proof instead, and even GPT-5.5 tops out near 75 — automated grading barely catches the bad ones.

cards.title: WILDTRACE: Benchmarking Natural Evidence Trails in Long-Context Reasoning
cards.hook: Most long-context tests plant a fake 'needle' in a haystack. Real evidence doesn't look like that — passing needle tests may not mean a model can truly reason over a document.

cards.title: GigaWorld-1: World Models as Robot Policy Evaluators
cards.hook: Testing a robot policy for real means slow, costly rollouts. GigaWorld-1 asks whether a video world model can judge a policy instead — and finds visual realism is the wrong thing to optimize for.

cards.title: EdgeBench: Scaling Laws for Learning from Real Environments
cards.hook: Pretraining has scaling laws everyone knows by heart. This paper finds the first one for what happens after deployment — how fast agents actually improve from real-world experience.

cards.title: RuBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents — and Catching a Silent Model Swap
cards.hook: A benchmark of real customer-style bug reports written in Russian. Its most striking result isn't the leaderboard — it's catching a deployed product quietly swapping in a different model mid-task.

cards.title: TUA-Bench: Benchmarking General-Purpose Terminal Agents
cards.hook: 120 real terminal tasks — from email triage to PhD-level scientific workflows — show even Claude Opus 4.8 tops out around 66%, far from reliable general computer use.

cards.title: Multi-LCB: Code Eval Beyond Python
cards.hook: LiveCodeBench keeps coding evals contamination-free — but only in Python. Multi-LCB extends it to twelve languages and finds models that look strong are quietly overfit to Python.

cards.title: When Your Top Feature Makes Predictions Worse
cards.hook: A feature can top your model's importance ranking and still hurt accuracy. The only way to be sure it helps: delete it, retrain, and compare on held-out data.

cards.title: Cross-Validation
cards.hook: One lucky or unlucky split can flatter or sink your model. Rotate the holdout and average — that's cross-validation.

cards.title: Phantom Gains: Auditing Self-Improvement Against a Measured Null
cards.hook: Run a frozen, untrained model through your self-improvement pipeline and it appears to gain and lose capabilities. Without that control, seven common measurement habits invert their own findings.

cards.title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
cards.hook: If an LLM's answer is a real probability estimate, slicing a population into subgroups and recombining should match asking about the whole. It usually doesn't — finer-grained is more accurate.

cards.title: LAION-BVD: 10 Million Hours of Open Video
cards.hook: 1.3 billion video URLs mined from CommonCrawl, 80 million downloaded, synthetically captioned for video, audio, and image pretraining — and released openly.

cards.title: Don't Trust the Label: License Laundering in AI Supply Chains
cards.hook: Licenses are supposed to travel with AI datasets and models — but across 232,270 supply-chain paths, obligation-bearing licenses survive end-to-end under 7% of the time.

cards.title: ImageNet: The Dataset That Sparked Deep Learning
cards.hook: A hand-labeled hoard of millions of images turned into the contest that, in 2012, lit the fuse on the deep learning era.

cards.title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
cards.hook: Most pretraining-poisoning research injects fake Wikipedia edits — a toy case next to messy web-scale reality. This paper shows public discussion forums are a real, live vector for attacking LLM pretraining data.

cards.title: LAION-5B: Open Image-Text at Scale
cards.hook: CLIP and DALL-E showed huge, noisy image-text data is gold. LAION-5B made that public — billions of CLIP-filtered pairs anyone can train open models on.

cards.title: The Pile: 800GB of Diverse Text
cards.hook: Web text alone leaves gaps. The Pile stitches together 22 curated sources — academic and professional — so a language model picks up knowledge plain web crawls miss.

cards.title: LibriBrain100: 100 Hours of MEG Data for Neural Speech Decoding
cards.hook: Most brain-decoding datasets go wide across many subjects. This one goes deep — ~80 hours inside a single brain — to test whether depth beats breadth.

cards.title: How Many Times Should You Repeat Your Best Data?
cards.hook: Good domain data doesn't scale like web crawl, so it gets diluted as models grow. How often can you repeat it before overfitting? The answer tracks the domain's loss, not its size.

cards.title: Models Can Pass the Exam Without Knowing the Syllabus
cards.hook: Educational benchmarks test whether a model answers school questions. This one tests whether it knows which concept comes before which — and the best model scores 57%.

cards.title: Moving Alphabet: A Controlled Study of Training Data for Text-to-Video Generation
cards.hook: Text-to-video research chases bigger architectures; this controlled study shows the training data decides the outcome — caption quality alone can cap what the model learns.

cards.title: UltraX: Refining Pre-Training Data at Scale with Adaptive Programmatic Editing
cards.hook: Rule-based data cleaning is too rigid; LLM rewrites are too slow at pretraining scale. UltraX teaches a model to emit structured, executable edit programs instead — insertions included.

cards.title: NVIDIA Opens 10T Tokens of Synthetic Data for Agentic AI
cards.hook: Real agent behavior needs data on tool failures and recovery paths that companies rarely want to share — NVIDIA's answer is 10+ trillion tokens of synthetic data built to stand in for it.

cards.title: Photoroom's Data Lesson: Caption Quality Rivals Architecture
cards.hook: Photoroom re-captioned their pretraining set with a VLM — longer, more accurate captions moved image FID from 21 to 13, a bigger jump than most architecture changes deliver.

cards.title: DataClaw0: Data Refinement as a Learnable Skill
cards.hook: Instead of scrubbing data with fixed rules, what if an agent learned to tailor it? DataClaw0 turns data refinement into a trainable skill judged by how well models train on its output.

cards.title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes LMs Better
cards.hook: Training corpora are full of copies — one 61-word sentence shows up 60,000+ times in C4. Strip the duplicates and models memorize far less and evaluate more honestly.

cards.title: Linear Regression
cards.hook: Predict a number by fitting a straight line through your data - the simplest model in ML and the mental blueprint for almost everything that came after.

cards.title: Logistic Regression
cards.hook: Take linear regression, squash its output through a sigmoid, and you get a probability - turning a number-predictor into a classifier with one extra step.

cards.title: Regularization: Ridge & Lasso
cards.hook: Add a penalty for large weights during training and your model learns to generalize instead of memorizing - Ridge shrinks, Lasso cuts.

cards.title: Decision Trees
cards.hook: A decision tree asks a series of yes/no questions about your data and follows the answers to a prediction - it learns which questions to ask from the training set.

cards.title: XGBoost: Scalable Tree Boosting
cards.hook: Boosting builds an ensemble one tree at a time, each tree correcting the mistakes of all the ones before it - XGBoost made this fast enough to dominate competitions.

cards.title: Random Forests
cards.hook: Grow hundreds of slightly different decision trees and average their votes - the crowd is smarter than any individual tree, and much harder to overfit.

cards.title: k-Nearest Neighbors
cards.hook: The laziest classifier: to label a new point, just find its k closest neighbors in the training set and take a vote - no training required at all.

cards.title: Support-Vector Networks (SVMs)
cards.hook: An SVM draws the decision boundary that maximizes the gap to the nearest training points - the wider the margin, the better it generalizes to new data.

cards.title: The Kernel Trick
cards.hook: Instead of explicitly mapping data into a high-dimensional space, just define a function that computes similarities as if you had - and you get nonlinear learning for free.

cards.title: k-Means Clustering
cards.hook: Pick k cluster centers, assign every point to the nearest one, move each center to the mean of its points, repeat - clusters emerge without any labels.

cards.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
cards.hook: Find the directions your data varies most, then keep only the top few - you compress many correlated features into a handful while retaining most of the signal.

cards.title: t-SNE & UMAP: Visualizing High-Dimensional Data
cards.hook: t-SNE and UMAP squeeze thousands of dimensions into two so you can see whether your model's internal representations form meaningful clusters.

cards.title: UMAP's Forgotten Graph: Network Science for Free Sensemaking
cards.hook: Everyone uses UMAP for its 2D scatter plot and throws away the graph it builds along the way — a graph that's still faithful to the data manifold, and worth analyzing on its own.

cards.title: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero (Karpathy)
cards.hook: Andrej Karpathy builds neural nets from nothing — line by line in code — until you've coded your own working GPT. Free.

cards.title: Automatic Differentiation
cards.hook: Backprop is one instance of a general trick: autodiff computes exact derivatives of any program by composing the chain rule — the engine inside every deep-learning framework.

cards.title: Activation Functions: ReLU & Friends
cards.hook: Stack linear layers and you still just have one linear layer. The nonlinearity between them is what gives a network its power.

cards.title: Transforming Rank: How Architecture Navigates the Spectral Pathologies of Depth
cards.hook: Skip connections and normalization are usually explained as controlling magnitude. Reframe them as controlling how much rank survives depth, and Pre-Norm's edge over Post-Norm falls out.

cards.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep CNNs (AlexNet)
cards.hook: In 2012 a single deep CNN trained on two GPUs crushed the ImageNet contest by a wide margin — and kicked off the deep learning era.

cards.title: ImageNet: The Dataset That Sparked Deep Learning
cards.hook: A hand-labeled hoard of millions of images turned into the contest that, in 2012, lit the fuse on the deep learning era.

cards.title: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet)
cards.hook: Stacking more layers used to make networks worse, not better. ResNet's fix — let each layer learn a tweak to its input — unlocked nets over 100 layers deep.

cards.title: U-Net: Encoder–Decoder for Segmentation
cards.hook: A U-shaped net that shrinks an image down to capture context, then rebuilds it pixel by pixel — with shortcuts that preserve fine detail. Now the workhorse inside diffusion models.

cards.title: Disentangling a Convolutional Neuron by Clustering What It Actually Detects
cards.hook: A single 'car detector' neuron might really be several overlapping detectors wearing one name. Clustering what it responds to pulls apart clean, monosemantic patterns hiding inside.

cards.title: RNNs, LSTMs & Sequences
cards.hook: To read a sequence, a network can loop over it one step at a time, carrying a memory of what came before. Plain RNNs forget fast; LSTMs add gates so they remember longer.

cards.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning
cards.hook: Translate a sentence by reading it into one vector, then writing a new sentence out of that vector. This encoder–decoder recipe powered early neural machine translation.

cards.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
cards.hook: Cramming a whole sentence into one vector loses information. This 2014 paper let the decoder look back at relevant source words at each step — the original attention mechanism.

cards.title: OmniOpt: A Taxonomy and Benchmark of 100+ Optimizers
cards.hook: Choosing an optimizer for training a large model is now a system-level design decision, but the field has 100+ methods and no shared map. This paper builds one — and a benchmark to go with it.

cards.title: Dropout: Preventing Overfitting by Dropping Units
cards.hook: Randomly delete units during each training step and you stop neurons from co-adapting - which is secretly like training a huge ensemble of thinned networks and averaging them at test time.

cards.title: Mixed Precision Training
cards.hook: Store weights, activations, and gradients in 16-bit floats to roughly halve memory - but keep a 32-bit master copy of the weights and scale the loss so tiny gradients don't vanish.

cards.title: Adam: The Default Optimizer
cards.hook: Adam gives every parameter its own adaptive step size by tracking the gradient's recent average and spread — and it mostly just works.

cards.title: Batch Normalization
cards.hook: Re-center and re-scale each layer's activations on every minibatch, and deep nets suddenly train faster and tolerate much higher learning rates.

cards.title: TorchJD: Stop Averaging Your Losses, Aggregate Their Gradients
cards.hook: Multi-task training usually blends losses into one number before taking a gradient step. TorchJD instead keeps every loss's own gradient and combines them so each one actually goes down.

cards.title: Effective Learning Rate Governs Loss Dynamics
cards.hook: Two pretraining runs with very different learning rates and weight norms trace the same loss curve — if the ratio between them matches. That ratio is the coordinate that matters.

cards.title: WarpSAC: Off-Policy RL Stabilizers Depend on the Data Regime
cards.hook: Massively parallel simulation broke the assumptions behind a decade of RL stabilizers. WarpSAC's finding: tricks that rescue data-starved training actively hold you back when data is abundant.

cards.title: Why Adam Beats SGD on Transformers: A Hessian Story
cards.hook: Adam is the default optimizer for LLMs and nobody could quite say why. This thesis traces it to the shape the Hessian takes during transformer training — and gets Adam-mini out of the explanation.

cards.title: Transforming Rank: How Architecture Navigates the Spectral Pathologies of Depth
cards.hook: Skip connections and normalization are usually explained as controlling magnitude. Reframe them as controlling how much rank survives depth, and Pre-Norm's edge over Post-Norm falls out.

cards.title: Scaling Laws for Learning Rate and Batch Size
cards.hook: Chinchilla told you how many tokens. This tells you what learning rate and batch size to use as you get there — including whether the optimum survives the decay phase.

cards.title: The Loss Doesn't See the Basis, But Adam Does
cards.hook: A factored model's loss can't tell which basis you wrote the factors in — but Adam's per-coordinate scaling can. That asymmetry predicts which optimizers keep gradient descent's low-rank bias.

cards.title: xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections
cards.hook: Hyper-Connections let a transformer keep several parallel residual streams instead of one — a big win from 1 to 4 streams, then a wall. xHC breaks the wall, scaling cleanly to 16 on real MoE models.

cards.title: On the Convergence of Adam, Revisited
cards.hook: A 2018 result showed Adam can fail to converge only in a specific hyperparameter regime. This paper shows it can fail for ANY choice — a flaw that spreads to AdamW, RMSProp, even Muon.

cards.title: One-Step Gradient Delay Isn't a Barrier — With the Right Optimizer
cards.hook: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism kills GPU idle time during pretraining — the field avoided it fearing instability, but that turns out to be an AdamW problem, not a fundamental one.

cards.title: Predictive Coding as a Backprop Alternative (Deepity)
cards.hook: Backprop isn't the only way to assign credit in a neural net. A hobby C++ library reports predictive coding matching it on MNIST — once you make the slow part fast.

cards.title: AdamW: Decoupled Weight Decay
cards.hook: L2 regularization and weight decay are the same thing for plain SGD - but not for Adam. Decoupling them fixes Adam's generalization and makes the best decay value independent of the learning rate.

cards.title: Muon: An Optimizer for Hidden Layers
cards.hook: Muon orthogonalizes each gradient update before applying it — and trained networks faster than AdamW, the first serious challenger to Adam's reign in years.

cards.title: Spectral Allocation: Why Muon Outperforms Adam, and How to Improve Muon
cards.hook: Probe a transformer's loss landscape direction by direction and a pattern appears: a few volatile directions demand tiny steps, the bulk tolerates far larger. That explains Muon > Adam > SGD.

cards.title: Dion3: Making Muon's Orthogonalization Cheap
cards.hook: Muon trains faster than AdamW but pays for it in a cubic-time orthogonalization step. Dion3 attacks that overhead at every layer of the stack — up to 6x faster optimizer steps at matching loss.

cards.title: Why Muon Skips Gradient Descent's Slow Start
cards.hook: Small-init gradient descent crawls through a 'saddle-to-saddle' bottleneck — Muon skips it, learning every mode at once and staying stable past where gradient descent blows up.

cards.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
cards.hook: Cramming a whole sentence into one vector loses information. This 2014 paper let the decoder look back at relevant source words at each step — the original attention mechanism.

cards.title: Sliding Window Beats Linear Attention
cards.hook: The cheap baseline nobody bothered to run wins: sliding-window attention with sinks matches or beats retrofitted linear-attention models, and needs no post-training at all.

cards.title: MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA)
cards.hook: Quadratic attention chokes at a million tokens. MiniMax runs exact attention over only a Top-k of key-value blocks per query group — cutting per-token attention compute ~28x at 1M context.

cards.title: What Is Attention?
cards.hook: Attention lets a model decide what to focus on: it scores how relevant each piece of input is to the current question, then blends them by those scores.

cards.title: HiLS Attention: Learning Chunk Selection for Near-Infinite Context
cards.hook: Sparse attention never quite matched full attention because chunk selection was a heuristic. This version trains chunk selection end-to-end — then extrapolates 64x past its training length.

cards.title: Grouped Query Experts: MoE Inside Attention
cards.hook: Mixture-of-experts usually routes whole feed-forward layers. Grouped Query Experts routes attention query heads instead — matching a dense baseline while firing half of them per token.

cards.title: The Mask Is Not the Model: Auditing Causality Leaks
cards.hook: Your attention mask can be perfectly correct and your model still peeks at the future. Two forward passes find the leak — and turned up real defects in Zamba2 and Nemotron-H.

cards.title: RoPE: Rotary Position Embedding
cards.hook: Encode position by rotating query/key vectors - relative distances then fall out of the dot product for free, no extra tokens or additive embeddings needed.

cards.title: Fast Weight Attention: Which Pair Is the Memory Learning From?
cards.hook: If a recurrent state is really an online learner, then what it trains on matters. This paper argues most fast-weight rules quietly use the wrong (key, value) pair.

cards.title: Sigmoid Attention Makes KV Eviction Stick
cards.hook: Learned cache-eviction gates train softly but must delete hard at inference. Swap softmax for sigmoid attention and that jump stops hurting — even though sigmoid is the worse LM.

cards.title: SparsePR: Training-Free Sparse Attention for Video Generation
cards.hook: Skipping attention blocks in a video model is cheap; knowing what you threw away is the hard part. SparsePR partitions queries by response and then reconstructs the missing residual.

cards.title: Frontier Language Models Struggle to Copy: Text Can Be Better Viewed in 2D
cards.hook: LLMs can solve hard reasoning problems in seconds but fumble at exactly copying text in their own context. The culprit: positional encodings biased toward shortcuts, fixed by laying text out in 2D.

cards.title: The Annotated Transformer
cards.hook: Want to truly get multi-head attention? Read the Transformer paper line by line — next to runnable PyTorch that implements every equation.

cards.title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
cards.hook: Split the difference between multi-head and multi-query attention: share KV heads across groups of query heads and get most of the memory savings with little quality loss.

cards.title: Multi-Query Attention: Faster Decoding
cards.hook: Share one key/value head across all query heads - the KV cache shrinks by a factor of H and decoding gets dramatically faster with barely any quality cost.

cards.title: The Illustrated Transformer
cards.hook: Before you tackle the Transformer paper, watch a sentence flow through one — query, key, value, and all — in clear pictures.

cards.title: Attention Is All You Need
cards.hook: Drop recurrence and convolution, keep only attention — and you get a model that trains in parallel and powers nearly every LLM since.

cards.title: Full-Bandwidth Transformer: Feed the Hidden State Back
cards.hook: Between decoding steps a transformer throws away everything except the sampled token. Widening that channel with the top-layer hidden state buys roughly 1.5x the training tokens' worth of quality.

cards.title: Compile a Transformer Instead of Training One
cards.hook: Write a computation graph in ordinary Python and get back the weights of a vanilla transformer that executes it — a real Phi-3 checkpoint, with zero gradient steps anywhere in the pipeline.

cards.title: Frontier Language Models Struggle to Copy: Text Can Be Better Viewed in 2D
cards.hook: LLMs can solve hard reasoning problems in seconds but fumble at exactly copying text in their own context. The culprit: positional encodings biased toward shortcuts, fixed by laying text out in 2D.

cards.title: FlashAttention: Fast, Memory-Efficient Exact Attention
cards.hook: Attention got faster not by approximating it, but by being smarter about GPU memory — never writing the giant attention matrix out to slow memory.

cards.title: The Annotated Transformer
cards.hook: Want to truly get multi-head attention? Read the Transformer paper line by line — next to runnable PyTorch that implements every equation.

cards.title: T5: Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer
cards.hook: What if translation, classification, and summarization were all just text-in, text-out? T5 makes one model and one recipe handle them all.

cards.title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
cards.hook: Recurrent depth helps most where tool use is actually hard: chaining calls, holding intermediate state, keeping dependencies straight. Single API calls barely notice.

cards.title: Loop the Loopies!
cards.hook: Looping a Transformer instead of growing it usually loses to just adding more parameters — Loopie is the looped MoE model that finally breaks that pattern, with IMO/IPhO gold-level reasoning.

cards.title: Next-Latent Prediction: Beyond Next-Token
cards.hook: Microsoft's NextLat teaches a transformer to predict its own next hidden state, not just the next token - building a compact internal world model and decoding up to 3.3x faster.

cards.title: T^2MLR: Transformer with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence
cards.hook: Decoding squeezes a transformer's thinking through token space each step. T2MLR pipes a cached middle-layer state into the next pass — recurring 20% of the network often beats looping it all.

cards.title: The State-Prediction Separation Hypothesis
cards.hook: A transformer uses one stream to both predict the next token and carry state for future predictions — split those two jobs apart, and the model gets measurably better.

cards.title: Gated Recurrent Transformers: Buying Depth with Recurrence
cards.hook: Sharing one transformer block across many layers saves memory but flattens the model. Add a GRU-style update gate and the same three layers can act like twelve.

cards.title: Which Tasks Do Transformers Extrapolate To? Now Decidable
cards.hook: Transformers sometimes handle sequences longer than they trained on, sometimes not. For regular languages there's now a complete characterization — and a polynomial-time algorithm to check.

cards.title: DiffusionGemma: Generating Text by Denoising, Not Decoding
cards.hook: DeepMind's DiffusionGemma generates text by refining a whole sequence in parallel instead of one token at a time — which the team reports is about 4x faster than standard autoregressive decoding.

cards.title: SANA-Video 2.0: Softmax Where It Counts
cards.hook: Pure linear attention is cheap but loses full-rank token mixing. SANA-Video 2.0 sprinkles softmax anchors back in at a 3:1 ratio and reaches softmax-level video quality at linear-attention cost.

cards.title: Nunchaku: 4-bit Diffusion Inference in Diffusers
cards.hook: Diffusion models hate 4-bit — activation outliers wreck image quality. SVDQuant peels the hardest weights into a tiny 16-bit low-rank branch, and Nunchaku now runs it inside Diffusers.

cards.title: iLLaDA: Improved Large Language Diffusion Models
cards.hook: An 8B language model trained from scratch with full bidirectional attention and a masked-diffusion objective — no autoregression — that holds its own against same-size autoregressive LLMs.

cards.title: DALL·E 2 (unCLIP): Text-to-Image with CLIP Latents
cards.hook: Turn a prompt into a CLIP image embedding first, then diffusion-decode that embedding into a picture. A two-stage path from words to vivid, editable images.

cards.title: U-Net: Encoder–Decoder for Segmentation
cards.hook: A U-shaped net that shrinks an image down to capture context, then rebuilds it pixel by pixel — with shortcuts that preserve fine detail. Now the workhorse inside diffusion models.

cards.title: Stereo2Spatial: Upmixing Stereo Music to 7.1.4 Spatial Audio with Flow-Matching Diffusion
cards.hook: A hobbyist project trains a flow-matching diffusion model to turn ordinary stereo music into full 7.1.4 spatial mixes — built on a dedicated VAE latent space rather than working directly on audio.

cards.title: NVIDIA Nemotron-TwoTower: A Diffusion-Based Language Model
cards.hook: NVIDIA's open Nemotron-TwoTower bolts a diffusion 'denoiser' tower onto a frozen autoregressive model to fill token blocks in parallel — reportedly 2.42x faster at ~98.7% of baseline quality.

cards.title: PerceptionDLM: Parallel Region Perception with Diffusion
cards.hook: Captioning ten regions of an image one at a time is slow. PerceptionDLM uses a diffusion language model's parallel decoding to describe them all at once.

cards.title: Moebius: 0.2B Inpainting Rivaling 10B
cards.hook: A 0.22B image-inpainting model that matches an 11.9B generalist (FLUX.1-Fill-Dev) — under 2% of the parameters and 15x faster — by pairing a linear-interaction backbone with latent-space distillation.

cards.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
cards.hook: Wreck an image into pure static one tiny step at a time, then train a network to undo it. Run the undo from random noise and you get a brand-new image.

cards.title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
cards.hook: Standard diffusion models are told which denoising step they're on; diffusion language models aren't — yet they track it anyway, a hidden clock you can read off their activations and even steer.

cards.title: The Seriality Gap in Video Diffusion Models
cards.hook: Give a video diffusion model more denoising steps and you'd expect better predictions on chains of causal events. Instead performance keeps degrading — the steps don't add real serial computation.

cards.title: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion: One Model, Three Decoding Modes
cards.hook: Instead of picking autoregressive or diffusion decoding, Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion trains one model to do both — plus a self-speculation mode that decodes up to 6x more tokens per forward pass.

cards.title: SynCity 3000: Scene-Scale 3D Generation from One Prompt
cards.hook: 3D generators are great at single objects but fall apart at scene scale. SynCity 3000 turns an image-to-3D generator into a convolution you can slide across an entire scene.

cards.title: VAE: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
cards.hook: Don't just compress data to a point — compress it to a distribution. That gives a smooth latent space you can sample from to generate genuinely new data.

cards.title: Ring Forcing: Teaching Video Models Object Permanence
cards.hook: Long video generation breaks in two ways at once: models forget what an object looked like, and can't reach far enough back to check. Ring Forcing attacks both.

cards.title: Simplax: Enriching Discrete Diffusion Without Changing Its Noise
cards.hook: Discrete diffusion is boxed in by its corruption kernel. Simplax bolts a continuous simplex variable onto each noisy token — richer training signal, same underlying categorical process.

cards.title: Flex-Forcing: One Video Diffusion Model, Two Inference Modes
cards.hook: Video diffusion models used to force a choice: globally coherent but slow, or fast streaming that drifts apart. Flex-Forcing chunks time and denoising steps together so one model does both.

cards.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion (Stable Diffusion)
cards.hook: Running diffusion on raw pixels is brutally expensive. Do it in a compressed latent space instead, and high-res text-to-image becomes cheap enough to run on a consumer GPU.

cards.title: Imagen: Photorealistic Text-to-Image Diffusion
cards.hook: Google found that a large frozen T5 text encoder matters more than a bigger image diffusion model - scaling language understanding is the key lever for photorealistic generation.

cards.title: Classifier-Free Guidance
cards.hook: Want a diffusion model to follow your prompt more closely? Blend its prompt-aware and prompt-blind predictions — no extra classifier required. That's the guidance-scale slider.

cards.title: What Does a Discrete Diffusion Model Learn?
cards.hook: A discrete diffusion model can be read as a denoiser, a score, or a bridge predictor. This paper proves they're the same optimum in different coordinates — with one exact best solution.

cards.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
cards.hook: Pit two networks against each other — a forger making fakes and a detective catching them — and the forger gets so good its fakes look real.

cards.title: StyleGAN: Controllable Image Synthesis
cards.hook: A GAN that generates photorealistic faces of people who don't exist — and lets you dial features at different scales, from face shape down to freckles.

cards.title: CycleGAN: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
cards.hook: Translate horses to zebras without a single matched pair - a cycle-consistency constraint does the work that paired data used to do.

cards.title: Pix2Pix: Image-to-Image Translation with Conditional GANs
cards.hook: Give a GAN paired input-output images and it learns a general recipe for translating any image domain to another - sketch to photo, map to satellite, day to night.

cards.title: What Are State-Space Models?
cards.hook: A compact hidden state summarizes everything seen so far - update it with each new input and you get sequence modeling that scales linearly, not quadratically.

cards.title: Nemotron-Labs-3-Puzzle-75B-A9B: Shrinking a 120B Model Without Retraining From Scratch
cards.hook: NVIDIA compressed its 120B-A12B Nemotron model down to 75B-A9B using 'Iterative Puzzle,' a post-training framework aimed at squeezing more inference efficiency out of an already-trained model.

cards.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
cards.hook: Make the state-space transitions depend on the input itself, add a hardware-aware scan, and you get a linear-time sequence model that matches Transformers on language - with no KV cache.

cards.title: The Mask Is Not the Model: Auditing Causality Leaks
cards.hook: Your attention mask can be perfectly correct and your model still peeks at the future. Two forward passes find the leak — and turned up real defects in Zamba2 and Nemotron-H.

cards.title: E²-TTT: Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training
cards.hook: Test-time training updates weights while it reads, but chunking for speed throws away the update's temporal structure. A closed-form state transition gets both.

cards.title: Nemotron 3 Ultra: Open Hybrid Mamba-Attention MoE
cards.hook: NVIDIA's open 550B model interleaves Mamba and attention inside a Mixture-of-Experts - hitting ~6x the inference throughput of comparable LLMs at on-par accuracy.

cards.title: S4: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces
cards.hook: A clever matrix parameterization turns the notoriously unstable state-space recurrence into a stable, fast sequence model that handles sequences 100x longer than Transformers.

cards.title: Fast Weight Attention: Which Pair Is the Memory Learning From?
cards.hook: If a recurrent state is really an online learner, then what it trains on matters. This paper argues most fast-weight rules quietly use the wrong (key, value) pair.

cards.title: Massive Activations Line Up With the Attention Layers
cards.hook: Hybrid linear-attention models have huge outlier activations too — and they aren't random. They spike right before every full-attention layer and plateau across the linear ones in between.

cards.title: Subquadratic Architectures: xLSTM vs. Mamba-2 vs. Gated DeltaNet
cards.hook: Transformers pay a quadratic tax on sequence length. Pitting xLSTM, Mamba-2, and Gated DeltaNet head-to-head on hard tasks, xLSTM comes out ahead — and the paper explains why.

cards.title: Attention Amnesia: When Chain-of-Thought Tuning Breaks Long-Range Recall
cards.hook: Fine-tuning a hybrid LLM on chain-of-thought makes it reason better but quietly forget how to find a needle in a long haystack — and the fix is to just copy back two weight matrices.

cards.title: Feature Learning in Gated Delta Networks at Scale
cards.hook: muP lets you tune hyperparameters on a small model and transfer them to a huge one. This paper derives the equivalent rules for gated delta networks, so sub-quadratic models scale without re-tuning.

cards.title: LongCat 2.0: A 1.6T-Parameter Open Model Under MIT License
cards.hook: 1.6 trillion total parameters, ~48B active, and released under the MIT license — one of the most permissively licensed large open-weight MoE models yet.

cards.title: Tencent Hy3: A 295B Open MoE Model Under Apache 2.0
cards.hook: Tencent's new Hy3 model switched from a restrictive community license to Apache 2.0 — removing the regional-use carve-outs that blocked adoption in the EU, UK, and South Korea.

cards.title: Audex: A Unified Audio-Text LLM That Doesn't Forget How to Think
cards.hook: Bolting audio onto a strong text model usually costs some of its reasoning. NVIDIA's Audex treats speech and text as one token stream, reporting top audio skills with little to no loss on text.

cards.title: Scaling the Horizon, Not the Parameters
cards.hook: A 35B mixture-of-experts agent matches trillion-parameter models on long-horizon tasks — by scaling how long its trajectories run, not how big its weights are.

cards.title: What Is a Mixture of Experts?
cards.hook: Instead of running every input through one big network, route each token to a few specialist sub-networks - total capacity grows without proportional compute.

cards.title: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: MoE Plus an N-Gram Table
cards.hook: An imminent Qwen release pairs a sparse ~125B-A6B mixture-of-experts with a 51B n-gram component — an unusual hybrid the local community thinks will fit on one machine.

cards.title: Motif 3: 314B Parameters, 13.2B Awake
cards.hook: A 314B-parameter MoE that only lights up 13.2B per token, built on 384 experts per layer and a hybrid attention scheme that folds differential attention into compressed KV.

cards.title: Grouped Query Experts: MoE Inside Attention
cards.hook: Mixture-of-experts usually routes whole feed-forward layers. Grouped Query Experts routes attention query heads instead — matching a dense baseline while firing half of them per token.

cards.title: LingBot-Video: A Sparse-MoE Video Diffusion World Model
cards.hook: Video diffusion models are usually dense — every parameter fires on every frame. LingBot-Video swaps in a sparse Mixture-of-Experts, then grades its own physics with a VLM judge.

cards.title: Compute-Efficient Hyperparameter Transfer for Large MoEs
cards.hook: Sweeping learning rates at trillion-token scale is unaffordable. Transfer across width with muP, then extrapolate along tokens with a fitted scaling law — and trust it for the real run.

cards.title: RARE: Steering MoE Models Without Breaking the Router
cards.hook: Activation steering works on dense models and quietly fails on mixture-of-experts — because your steering vector also reroutes the tokens. Project it into the router's null space.

cards.title: Nemotron 3 Ultra: Open Hybrid Mamba-Attention MoE
cards.hook: NVIDIA's open 550B model interleaves Mamba and attention inside a Mixture-of-Experts - hitting ~6x the inference throughput of comparable LLMs at on-par accuracy.

cards.title: Redesigning MoE Routers with Manifold Power Iteration
cards.hook: An MoE router points each token at the right expert — yet nothing forces its rows to actually represent those experts. This aligns each router row with its expert's principal direction.

cards.title: CE-MoE: Fewer Expert Layers, Same Loss, a Third Less Compute
cards.hook: Interleaving an MoE layer after every attention block means paying all-to-all communication over and over. Concentrating experts in a few layers cut GPU-hours by a third at matched quality.

cards.title: xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections
cards.hook: Hyper-Connections let a transformer keep several parallel residual streams instead of one — a big win from 1 to 4 streams, then a wall. xHC breaks the wall, scaling cleanly to 16 on real MoE models.

cards.title: Mixture-of-Depths
cards.hook: Mixture-of-Depths lets a transformer spend more compute on some tokens than others — routing each token through, or around, layers within a fixed budget.

cards.title: DeepSeek-V4-Pro Ships for Real: 1.7T Under MIT
cards.hook: The preview is over. DeepSeek's 1.7-trillion-parameter MoE lands with open MIT weights, built-in speculative decoding, and benchmark claims aimed straight at the closed frontier.

cards.title: Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B Is Out
cards.hook: Qwen's next flagship landed after a week of countdown threads — and the name says it all: a sparse mixture-of-experts in the trillions, with under a hundred billion awake per token.

cards.title: Mixtral of Experts
cards.hook: Mixtral packs 8 experts per layer but routes each token through only 2, so you get the capacity of a ~47B model at the compute cost of a ~13B one - open weights included.

cards.title: FreeToken: Serving Frontier MoE Models on the Machine You Own
cards.hook: Instead of treating a laptop as a tiny datacenter GPU, FreeToken treats the whole machine as one elastic inference platform — and runs a 753B model on a single workstation card.

cards.title: Switch Transformer: Scaling to Trillion-Parameter Models
cards.hook: Route every token to exactly one expert instead of many - this single simplification made trillion-parameter MoE models stable enough to train at scale.

cards.title: Loop the Loopies!
cards.hook: Looping a Transformer instead of growing it usually loses to just adding more parameters — Loopie is the looped MoE model that finally breaks that pattern, with IMO/IPhO gold-level reasoning.

cards.title: Multi-Vector Retrieval: One Vector Per Token, Scored Late
cards.hook: Squeezing a document into one vector throws away where the match was. Late interaction keeps a vector per token and defers scoring — better recall, 42x the index.

cards.title: Word2Vec: Word Embeddings
cards.hook: Teach a model to predict a word's neighbors, and it quietly learns vectors where king minus man plus woman lands near queen.

cards.title: ZipTok3D: A 3D Tokenizer Where the First Token Already Says a Lot
cards.hook: Most 3D tokenizers fall apart when squeezed to a handful of tokens. ZipTok3D trains the leading tokens to carry the essential geometry — matching a 32-token baseline with one token.

cards.title: What an Engram Actually Is
cards.hook: The n-gram tables in new open models are not a trick for running 1T parameters off an SSD — they are an embedding table with a longer key, and that is a more interesting idea.

cards.title: Subword Tokenization with Byte-Pair Encoding
cards.hook: Whole words make a giant vocabulary; single characters make long sequences. Subwords split the difference — and let models read words they've never seen.

cards.title: SentencePiece: Language-Independent Tokenization
cards.hook: Most tokenizers assume you can split on spaces first. SentencePiece drops that assumption and tokenizes raw text directly — in any language.

cards.title: Distilling Across Different Tokenizers
cards.hook: On-policy distillation usually assumes teacher and student share a tokenizer. Map both into byte space and you can finally distil from a teacher whose vocabulary is nothing like yours.

cards.title: Training Your Own Late-Interaction Retriever
cards.hook: A domain-specific multi-vector retriever took 14.5 hours on one RTX 3090 and beat every zero-shot model tested — including dense retrievers 33 times its size.

cards.title: In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs
cards.hook: On-device models ship small vocabularies to save memory, so languages added later get shredded into extra tokens. This recipe grows the tokenizer after the fact — no retraining from scratch.

cards.title: Rate-Utility Frontiers for Language Encodings: Comparing Tokens, Bytes, and Pixels
cards.hook: Tokens, bytes, or pixels — which encodes language best? A controlled head-to-head across 13 languages finds no single winner: each encoding trades off differently by task.

cards.title: The Design Fundamentals of Pixel Text Representation Learning
cards.hook: What if a model read text as an image instead of tokens? Controlled ablations pin down the four ingredients that make pixel-space text encoders actually work.

cards.title: GPT-5.6: Frontier Intelligence That Scales With Your Ambition
cards.hook: GPT-5.6 ships as three tiers instead of one model — Luna, Terra, Sol — built around squeezing more capability out of every token rather than just scaling up.

cards.title: MiniMax Reportedly Plans a 2.7-Trillion-Parameter M3 Pro
cards.hook: MiniMax's current flagship already runs 428B parameters — sources now say the next one, codenamed M3 Pro, could jump to 2.7 trillion and still ship open-source as soon as Q3.

cards.title: GPT-5
cards.hook: GPT-5 folds OpenAI's two lines into one: a router decides on the fly whether a prompt needs a fast answer or deep step-by-step reasoning, so you stop picking models.

cards.title: gpt-oss: OpenAI's Open-Weight Models
cards.hook: OpenAI's first open-weight release since GPT-2: two Apache-2.0 reasoning models, the larger running on a single 80GB GPU and the smaller on a 16GB laptop.

cards.title: The Llama 4 Herd: Natively Multimodal, Mixture-of-Experts
cards.hook: Llama 4 is Meta's first mixture-of-experts family - only 17B parameters fire per token, but the full models hold hundreds of billions, and they read text, images, and video natively.

cards.title: BERT: Pretraining Deep Bidirectional Transformers
cards.hook: What if a model read a sentence both directions at once? BERT did, by masking words and predicting them — and made pretrain-then-fine-tune the default recipe in NLP.

cards.title: GPT-3: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
cards.hook: Show the model a few examples right in the prompt and it picks up the task — no fine-tuning, no gradient updates. GPT-3 turned prompting into the new programming.

cards.title: GLM-5.3: All the Gains From Post-Training
cards.hook: z.ai shipped GLM-5.3 on the same base model as GLM-5.2 — every improvement, including a claimed 50% jump on coding, comes from post-training alone.

cards.title: Puro-2B: Pretraining a Real LLM for $6,900
cards.hook: Reproducing SmolLM3-3B costs over $700K. This team pretrained a 2B model on 1.4T tokens using consumer RTX 5090s for under $6.9K — and released the whole recipe.

cards.title: Full-Bandwidth Transformer: Feed the Hidden State Back
cards.hook: Between decoding steps a transformer throws away everything except the sampled token. Widening that channel with the top-layer hidden state buys roughly 1.5x the training tokens' worth of quality.

cards.title: Synthetic Persona Pretraining: Alignment From Token Zero
cards.hook: Alignment is normally a coat of paint applied after pretraining. This work installs the assistant's values from the first token — and finds that the earlier you start, the deeper they hold.

cards.title: The Information Abundance Paradox: Long Context Can Undermine What a Model Knows
cards.hook: If the answer is always in the context window, the model stops bothering to learn it. Past an intermediate context length, more training context makes a model weaker without its crutch.

cards.title: Scalable Visual Pretraining for Language Intelligence
cards.hook: Documents pack meaning into layout, figures, and equations that plain text can't fully capture. Skip the OCR step: pretraining directly on rendered pages beats text-only pretraining.

cards.title: iLLaDA: Improved Large Language Diffusion Models
cards.hook: An 8B language model trained from scratch with full bidirectional attention and a masked-diffusion objective — no autoregression — that holds its own against same-size autoregressive LLMs.

cards.title: GLM-5.2
cards.hook: z.ai's GLM-5.2 became the strongest open-weights model of mid-2026 — the first reported to clear 80% on Terminal-Bench and a coding favorite that rivals top closed models at a fraction of the cost.

cards.title: Claude 4: Opus 4 and Sonnet 4
cards.hook: Claude 4 lets a model interleave reasoning with tool calls - thinking, calling a tool, thinking again, and even running tools in parallel - rather than reasoning once and answering.

cards.title: Claude Opus 4.5
cards.hook: Anthropic's Opus 4.5 pushed frontier coding and agentic tool use forward — and cut Opus pricing sharply, making the top tier far cheaper to run at scale.

cards.title: Grok 4
cards.hook: xAI's Grok 4 leaned hard on reinforcement learning and native tool use, topping several reasoning benchmarks at its July 2025 launch.

cards.title: Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence
cards.hook: Moonshot's Kimi K2 is a trillion-parameter open-weight Mixture-of-Experts model built agentic-first — and trained at that scale without a single loss spike using the MuonClip optimizer.

cards.title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
cards.hook: Meta released Llama 2 with open weights and a commercial-use license, giving anyone a strong RLHF-tuned chat model to build on - and kicked off a wave of open-LLM development.

cards.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
cards.hook: Meta's Llama 3 family, trained on roughly 15 trillion tokens with a 405B-parameter flagship, narrowed the gap to closed frontier models while staying open-weights.

cards.title: Qwen3: Hybrid Thinking, Open Weights
cards.hook: Qwen3 puts a reasoning switch in one model - a slow 'thinking' mode and a fast 'non-thinking' mode with a controllable budget - across a lineup that runs from 0.6B to a 235B MoE.

cards.title: FLAN: Instruction Tuning
cards.hook: Teach a model to follow many tasks phrased as plain instructions, and it learns to follow instructions for tasks it never saw — zero-shot.

cards.title: LLaMA: Open & Efficient Foundation Models
cards.hook: You don't need a 175B-parameter model to compete. LLaMA trained smaller models on lots of public data — and lit a fire under the open-weights community.

cards.title: T5: Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer
cards.hook: What if translation, classification, and summarization were all just text-in, text-out? T5 makes one model and one recipe handle them all.

cards.title: When Robot Data Can't Scale, Scale the Representation Instead
cards.hook: Web images scale; robot trajectories don't. VLAct argues the fix isn't more teleoperation but better use of it — and beats full-data baselines on an unseen humanoid using 20% of the trajectories.

cards.title: Granite 4.2: IBM's Open 3B/8B/30B Family
cards.hook: Three Apache-2.0 dense models with 512K context, trained through a five-phase pretrain, agentic SFT, and stacked GRPO runs — with the whole recipe written down.

cards.title: Qwen3.8-27B Has the Same Architecture as Qwen3.6-27B
cards.hook: A community diff of the two model configs came back with zero changes — so whatever Qwen3.8-27B gained over its predecessor came entirely from the training recipe.

cards.title: Small Models Are Enough to Imitate Human Choice Behaviour
cards.hook: Fourteen models from 135M to 14B were fine-tuned on 10.7 million human decisions. In-distribution, 0.6B matched a 70B baseline — scale only started paying off on unfamiliar tasks.

cards.title: UltraX: Refining Pre-Training Data at Scale with Adaptive Programmatic Editing
cards.hook: Rule-based data cleaning is too rigid; LLM rewrites are too slow at pretraining scale. UltraX teaches a model to emit structured, executable edit programs instead — insertions included.

cards.title: AutoTrainess: Teaching Language Models to Improve Language Models Autonomously
cards.hook: Training a model is more than writing code — AutoTrainess gives agents purpose-built interfaces for planning, data prep, and training runs, and clearly out-trains agents left in a raw CLI.

cards.title: Claude Opus 4.7: Frontier Coding (2026)
cards.hook: Claude Opus 4.7's gains land hardest on the hardest software-engineering tasks, and it now checks its own work - better self-verification of its outputs alongside the coding boost.

cards.title: GLM-4.6
cards.hook: Zhipu's GLM-4.6 is an open-weight MoE that became a popular drop-in coding backend — near Claude Sonnet 4 on real-world coding, with a 200K context and a permissive license.

cards.title: Mistral 7B
cards.hook: Mistral 7B outperforms much larger open models on most benchmarks - showing that architecture choices and data quality can stretch a 7B parameter budget a long way.

cards.title: Mistral Medium 3
cards.hook: Mistral Medium 3 chased frontier-class quality at a fraction of the cost — 'medium is the new large' — aimed squarely at enterprise deployment.

cards.title: OLMo 2: A Fully Open Model
cards.hook: Ai2's OLMo 2 is fully open — not just weights, but the training data, code, and checkpoints — the strongest reproducible-from-scratch model for researchers.

cards.title: Phi-3: A Capable Language Model on Your Phone
cards.hook: Microsoft's Phi-3 Mini matches much larger models on reasoning benchmarks by training on heavily filtered, 'textbook-quality' data - and is small enough to run on a phone.

cards.title: Ring-Zero: Scaling Zero RL to a Trillion Parameters for Emergent Reasoning
cards.hook: Zero RL — reasoning trained on verifiable rewards, no human labels — had only been tried small-scale. At a trillion parameters, the model starts inventing reasoning habits nobody hand-coded.

cards.title: A Formal Limit on What Any Model Can Learn From Text Alone
cards.hook: There is a ceiling on how well meaning can be recovered from the form of an utterance — and it holds for any text representation, no matter how much data or supervision produced it.

cards.title: Effective Learning Rate Governs Loss Dynamics
cards.hook: Two pretraining runs with very different learning rates and weight norms trace the same loss curve — if the ratio between them matches. That ratio is the coordinate that matters.

cards.title: Compute-Efficient Hyperparameter Transfer for Large MoEs
cards.hook: Sweeping learning rates at trillion-token scale is unaffordable. Transfer across width with muP, then extrapolate along tokens with a fitted scaling law — and trust it for the real run.

cards.title: Function-Aware Fill-in-the-Middle as Mid-Training for Coding Agent Foundation Models
cards.hook: Ordinary pretraining only sees code left-to-right. This mid-training trick masks whole functions like a tool call's return value — and it measurably makes coding agents better.

cards.title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
cards.hook: Labs rarely disclose their data mixture recipes — but WARP shows you can recover a fine-tuned model's training-domain proportions just from its released weights, no training data required.

cards.title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
cards.hook: DeepSeek-V3 trained a frontier-class MoE model for a fraction of the cost of comparable closed models, using FP8 training and a novel load-balancing scheme to make efficiency the headline result.

cards.title: DeepSeek-V4: Sparse Attention, Million-Token Default
cards.hook: DeepSeek-V4 makes a 1M-token context window the default and pairs token-wise compression with sparse attention, so long-context inference no longer pays the usual compute and memory tax.

cards.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
cards.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.

cards.title: Scaling Laws for Learning Rate and Batch Size
cards.hook: Chinchilla told you how many tokens. This tells you what learning rate and batch size to use as you get there — including whether the optimum survives the decay phase.

cards.title: Scaling Native Multimodal Pre-Training From Scratch
cards.hook: Chinchilla told you how to split compute between model size and tokens for text. This maps the same frontier for models trained on images and text from day one.

cards.title: Scaling Laws for Hypernetwork-Based Knowledge Injection
cards.hook: Instead of fine-tuning to memorize facts, train a hypernetwork to generate a LoRA adapter that injects them — and it follows clean scaling laws with steeper out-of-distribution gains.

cards.title: MiniMax-M1
cards.hook: MiniMax-M1 is an open-weight reasoning model with a million-token context and 'lightning attention' — and a hybrid design that made full RL training cost about $0.5M.

cards.title: GPT-4 Technical Report
cards.hook: GPT-4 clears the bar on a wide range of professional and academic benchmarks - passing the bar exam near the top of the score range, for instance - while accepting both text and images as input.

cards.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
cards.hook: Ask a big model to 'think step by step' and its math and logic scores jump. Reasoning was there all along — you just had to ask it to show its work.

cards.title: Chinchilla: Compute-Optimal Scaling
cards.hook: Most giant models were starved of data. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget you should grow parameters and tokens together — and a smaller, longer-trained model won.

cards.title: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
cards.hook: RL post-training is usually studied apart from pretraining. Using chess as a testbed, this paper shows post-RL performance is predictable from pretraining loss alone.

cards.title: Scaling Laws Break at the Edges — Because They Assume Size and Data Are Independent
cards.hook: Chinchilla-style laws mispredict loss when data is scarce or a model is heavily overtrained. Add one interaction exponent coupling capacity and data, and the error drops 1.5–3x.

cards.title: How Many Times Should You Repeat Your Best Data?
cards.hook: Good domain data doesn't scale like web crawl, so it gets diluted as models grow. How often can you repeat it before overfitting? The answer tracks the domain's loss, not its size.

cards.title: Does Telling an LLM to Be Concise Save Money?
cards.hook: Two ways to spend fewer tokens: shorten what you send, or shorten what you ask for back. Measured across nine models, only one of them actually saves you money.

cards.title: The Most Important Prompting Skill Is Knowing the Domain
cards.hook: LLMs let novices produce adequate work, which makes prompting look like it needs no skill. The argument here: the skill is domain expertise, and the human is usually the bottleneck.

cards.title: Skill Issue: Are Skills Language-Invariant in LLMs?
cards.hook: Have a model play a game against itself, one copy in English and one in another language. Same model, same rules, same board — and markedly different playing strength.

cards.title: Memory-Augmented Compression: Cheaper Chain-of-Thought
cards.hook: Compressing chain-of-thought saves tokens but breaks the logic. Move the reasoning into the prompt as reusable memory and you get the savings without the damage.

cards.title: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate?
cards.hook: LLM-as-a-Judge assumes evaluation is easier than generation — a controlled test finds the opposite on 3 of 4 benchmarks, and attention analysis shows why.

cards.title: In-Context Learning
cards.hook: Paste a few examples into a prompt and a large language model performs the task - no gradient updates, no fine-tuning, the prompt is the program.

cards.title: Large Language Models Are Zero-Shot Reasoners
cards.hook: Appending 'Let's think step by step' to a prompt unlocks multi-step reasoning with zero examples - chain-of-thought without the example-writing overhead.

cards.title: Naive Prompt Optimization Beats the Fancy Search
cards.hook: Prompt optimizers have grown elaborate search machinery. A single-lineage loop that just asks a teacher model to revise the prompt matches or beats GEPA with fewer rollouts.

cards.title: Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions?
cards.hook: Let an LLM write itself 'notes to self' — reusable strategies distilled from its own solution attempts — and its math and logic reasoning improves, with self-written notes as good as a teacher's.

cards.title: Hourglass Reasoning: Context Isolation for Rigorous Induction
cards.hook: Telling a model to state its inferred rule barely helps it self-refine. Forcing only a compressed rule — not the full trace — through a bottleneck nearly doubles a benchmark score.

cards.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
cards.hook: Sample the model many times, let each run reason its own way, then take the majority answer - diverse reasoning paths vote out individual errors.

cards.title: More Correct Mass, Worse Answers: Where Power Sampling Breaks
cards.hook: Sharpening a model's distribution can push more probability onto correct reasoning paths and still make the final answer worse — by up to 18.5 points. The culprit is coverage, not correctness.

cards.title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
cards.hook: If an LLM's answer is a real probability estimate, slicing a population into subgroups and recombining should match asking about the whole. It usually doesn't — finer-grained is more accurate.

cards.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute
cards.hook: A new scaling axis: instead of a bigger model, let a model think longer at inference — often a better use of compute, and the principle behind o1 and R1.

cards.title: Learning When to Think: Adaptive Test-Time Compute
cards.hook: Let the model pick its own thinking budget with its very first token. On MATH500 that cut response length 41% while accuracy barely moved.

cards.title: Refute, Don't Resample: Claim-Level Reliability Assessment
cards.hook: Refuting a wrong claim needs one decisive flaw; building a right answer needs a flawless path. CLR spends test-time compute on that asymmetry instead of on more samples.

cards.title: When More Sampling Hurts: The Modal Ceiling and Correlation Ceiling of Test-Time Scaling
cards.hook: Sample a reasoning model dozens of times and coverage keeps climbing — but picking the right answer from the pile plateaus fast, and extra samples past that point can backfire.

cards.title: ParaTempo: Steering Parallel Reasoning With Temporal Confidence
cards.hook: Exploring many solution paths at once makes reasoning models better and slower. ParaTempo watches how fast each branch converges on an answer and kills, retires, or forks branches on that one signal.

cards.title: Why RAG? Grounding LLMs in Your Data
cards.hook: An LLM only knows what it was trained on — until it's stale, private, or just wrong. RAG bolts on a search step so the model answers from your data and can cite it.

cards.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
cards.hook: Why force a model to memorize everything? RAG lets it look things up — fetch relevant documents, then answer from that evidence instead of frozen weights alone.

cards.title: Referential Dangling: How Prompt Compression Quietly Breaks Multi-Hop Answers
cards.hook: Compressors score chunks independently, so they can keep the sentence holding the answer and delete the one defining who it's about — leaving text that reads fine and answers wrong.

cards.title: Search Beyond What Can Be Taught: Evolving the Knowledge Boundary in Agentic Visual Generation
cards.hook: Ask an image generator for a real but obscure or brand-new entity, and it'll confidently draw the wrong thing. A new benchmark shows how bad that gets — and how to teach it to search instead.

cards.title: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR)
cards.hook: Keyword search misses answers that use different words. DPR embeds questions and passages into one vector space and retrieves by meaning — the backbone of modern vector search.

cards.title: CamoDocs: Poisoning RAG Without Leaving Fingerprints
cards.hook: Existing RAG poisoning attacks paste the target query into the malicious document, which is exactly what makes them easy to filter. CamoDocs hides the payload inside plausible benign text instead.

cards.title: RetrievalRouter: Pick the Retrieval Pipeline Per Query
cards.hook: Retrieval forces a choice between accurate-but-slow and fast-but-blind. A router reading only the query text claims both: 2.5% more accurate, 12.4x faster than the best static pipeline.

cards.title: EviRank: Turning Image Re-ranking Into a Checklist
cards.hook: "Find this shirt in pink" hides three instructions: keep the entity, change the attribute, ignore the background. EviRank makes each one an explicit, checkable criterion.

cards.title: AutoIndex: Learning Representation Programs for Retrieval
cards.hook: Stop tuning the retriever — tune the documents. AutoIndex searches for executable programs that rewrite and reorganize docs before indexing, lifting recall on every task with BM25 left untouched.

cards.title: EU AI Act OpenRAG: Chunking a Law by Its Legal Structure, Not Sliding Windows
cards.hook: Most RAG corpora chunk text with sliding character windows. This one chunks the EU AI Act by its actual legal structure and ships it as a single SQLite file.

cards.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Embed Ranks #1 Overall on RTEB
cards.hook: A new embedding model from NVIDIA takes the top overall spot on RTEB, the retrieval-focused benchmark — with an eye toward making agentic retrieval, not just search, more reliable.

cards.title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
cards.hook: Search agents forget what they've already tried and loop on failed queries, burning their budget. SearchOS gives them a shared, persistent memory of what's been searched, found, and failed.

cards.title: Deceptive Grounding: When RAG Cites the Right Text, Wrong Entity
cards.hook: A RAG system can pass every faithfulness, hallucination, and citation check while quietly citing the wrong entity's evidence — real text, real citation, wrong subject.

cards.title: WebSwarm: Recursive Multi-Agent Orchestration for Deep-and-Wide Web Search
