cards.hook: One long search trajectory can't be both deep and wide at once. WebSwarm lets the search tree grow instead: any node that can't solve its own piece just spawns children and waits for their evidence.

cards.title: Pitwall: Faithful Live Commentary via Claim Verification
cards.hook: Live sports commentary has no reference text to check against — facts change every few seconds. This production F1 system verifies every sentence against a live probability model before publishing.

cards.title: Why One Engineer Dropped Embeddings for BM25 in Tool Selection
cards.hook: An engineer running an agent with ~140 tools dropped embedding-based tool selection for plain BM25 — cosine similarity over short tool descriptions was dangerous in production.

cards.title: GraphRAG
cards.hook: GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from your documents first, then answers over its structure — so it can reason across many sources, not just retrieve the nearest few chunks.

cards.title: Why ColBERT-Style Retrieval Fails on Negation — and the Fix
cards.hook: Late-interaction retrieval (MaxSim, as in ColBERT) is provably as expressive as vector search for ordinary matches — but provably can't handle negation. Signed MaxSim closes that exact gap.

cards.title: Multi-Vector Retrieval: One Vector Per Token, Scored Late
cards.hook: Squeezing a document into one vector throws away where the match was. Late interaction keeps a vector per token and defers scoring — better recall, 42x the index.

cards.title: Training Your Own Late-Interaction Retriever
cards.hook: A domain-specific multi-vector retriever took 14.5 hours on one RTX 3090 and beat every zero-shot model tested — including dense retrievers 33 times its size.

cards.title: Muse Glimmer: a 30B Open-Weight Model Built for Always-On Local Agents
cards.hook: Meta released a 30B dense multimodal model under Apache 2.0, tuned for agents that run all day on your own machine — quantized to ~4-bit it fits under 20 GB.

cards.title: Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, and 3.5 Flash Cyber
cards.hook: Google splits its fast tier three ways: a workhorse that answers in fewer tokens, a 350-tokens-per-second speed model, and a security specialist locked behind a government pilot.

cards.title: Kimi K3: Moonshot's 2.8T-Parameter Successor Goes Live
cards.hook: Moonshot's Kimi K3 lands on web and app with 2.8 trillion parameters and a 1-million-token context — nearly 3x K2's scale, aimed squarely at coding and agentic work.

cards.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): A Standard for Connecting LLMs to Tools
cards.hook: MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how AI applications expose tools, data, and resources to models - think USB-C for AI tool integrations.

cards.title: Self-Improvements in Modern Agentic Systems: A Survey
cards.hook: Self-improving agents are leaving the lab for production. This survey, co-authored by Jürgen Schmidhuber, gives the field a shared vocabulary for what an agent can update about itself, and what drives that update.

cards.title: ChatGPT Work: An Agent That Delivers Finished Work
cards.hook: ChatGPT Work doesn't just chat — it reaches into your actual apps and files, grinds on a project for hours, and hands back a real spreadsheet or slide deck instead of a wall of text.

cards.title: Agentic Environment Engineering: A Survey
cards.hook: Agents only get as good as the worlds they practice in. This survey maps the full lifecycle of agent environments — how we model, synthesize, evaluate, and grow them.

cards.title: Zer0Fit: Zero-Shot Tabular ML and Forecasting, Callable by Any LLM
cards.hook: Instead of training a model on your spreadsheet, an agent can now just ask a foundation model to guess — and get scores close to a tuned one, no training loop involved.

cards.title: SecOPD: Token-Level Feedback Against Prompt Injection
cards.hook: Defensive fine-tuning keeps failing because DPO and GRPO grade a whole answer at once. Score each token instead and adaptive-injection success drops from 94% to 9%.

cards.title: Test-Time Scaling in the Wild: Choosing Is the Bottleneck, Not Generating
cards.hook: Spend more inference compute on open-ended tasks and the best candidate in your pool keeps getting better. The problem is you can't tell which one it is.

cards.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
cards.hook: Ask a big model to 'think step by step' and its math and logic scores jump. Reasoning was there all along — you just had to ask it to show its work.

cards.title: Verbalization Debt: What an LLM Loses When Its Subagent Has to Explain Itself in Words
cards.hook: In chess, robotics, and games the strongest agent isn't a language model. Wiring one into an LLM orchestrator means compressing its state into text — and that tax grows with scale.

cards.title: Writing the Physical World Down as Runnable Code
cards.hook: A VLM can describe a falling object without holding any model of what governs the fall. Code-as-World makes the model emit executable code as its world representation — then runs it to check itself.

cards.title: A Fake Dashboard Is Enough to Make an Agent Commit
cards.hook: Show an agent a professional-looking market panel and it will make a directional call on a provably unpredictable question — just as readily when every number on the panel is invented.

cards.title: LLMs Can Design Near-Optimal OR Algorithms
cards.hook: Given only a problem class description and a Python sandbox, a frontier model writes an algorithm that matches or beats the best known method — before ever seeing an evaluation instance.

cards.title: PILOT: Self-Improvement While the Run Is Still Going
cards.hook: Most agent self-improvement happens after the run ends, too late to save it. PILOT gives a supervisor the power to redirect or abort a live worker — and cuts output tokens by nearly half.

cards.title: When Tool Outputs Become Commands
cards.hook: Prompt injection into agents is really one confusion: the thing that suggests an action and the thing that authorizes it are treated as the same thing.

cards.title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion
cards.hook: Best agent configuration finished 20 of 97 real scientific workflows. And among failing Claude Code runs, 75.5% still signed off claiming they were done.

cards.title: Repair or Resample? Rethinking Failure Debugging in Multi-Agent Systems
cards.hook: Most multi-agent repair methods just rerun the trajectory and hope. Freeze the randomness and the truth comes out: unguided reruns reproduce only 68% of failures and fix under 7% of them.

cards.title: AgentMercury: Synthesizing Worlds, Not Tasks
cards.hook: Instead of building an environment per task, build a persistent business world with entities, services and invariants — and let the tasks fall out of it.

cards.title: Where to Spend Model Size in Self-Refinement
cards.hook: Generate, critique, revise — three stages, and most systems use the same big model for all three. The critic barely needs to be big; the reviser absolutely does.

cards.title: Bounded Agents: Delegation Security for Multi-Agent AI Systems
cards.hook: Prompt injection only matters if the agent had the authority to obey. Treat it as an authorization-architecture bug and enforce the limits outside the model.

cards.title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
cards.hook: Agents outgrow the environments we hand-build for them. Instead of writing new worlds, wrap the old one in a programmable layer that reshapes it around the agent's current weaknesses.

cards.title: Agent Memory Is a Dose, Not a Switch
cards.hook: IBM Research tested how much extracted guideline memory to give an agent. The right amount depends on the model: strong ones absorb everything, weaker ones do better with curated retrieval.

cards.title: How Agents Fail at Autonomous Research: The Missing Metacognitive Loop
cards.hook: 800 agent trajectories across 100 real frontier-science tasks converge on one deficit: agents don't check what they wrote against what they found.

cards.title: Agent Safety Should Be a Runtime Contract
cards.hook: Safety trained into the weights can't stop an agent that deletes a file or claims a test passed. This position paper argues the unit of safety is the trajectory, not the model.

cards.title: Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing?
cards.hook: Agent instruction files only ever get longer. The reason is asymmetric cost: adding a line is free, but deleting one whose rationale is lost risks a regression you can't cheaply check.

cards.title: Convergent Detour Hijacking: The Attack That Lets Your Agent Succeed
cards.hook: A malicious third-party skill doesn't have to break your agent's task. It can just take the scenic route — burning 67% more tokens and 92% more wall-clock while the final answer still looks correct.

cards.title: Distillation Without Training: Let a Strong Model Build the Weak One a Harness
cards.hook: A strong model writes the scaffolding — code, routing, format rules — and a weak model runs inside it. Average performance nearly doubled, 0.49 to 0.91, with no parameter updates at all.

cards.title: It Knows Both Facts and Still Can't Chain Them
cards.hook: A model can store 'A is B' and 'B is C' and still fail at 'what is A's C?'. Transformers trained from scratch show why: lower layers build the intermediate, upper layers don't reason over it.

cards.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability?
cards.hook: An agent score only means something if the task still requires the skill it claims to test. Auditing 2,385 traces, two-thirds showed the agent taking a shortcut instead.

cards.title: The Regression Tax on Agent Skills
cards.hook: Handing an agent a procedural skill doesn't only add wins — it also breaks tasks it used to solve. The best skills win by regressing less, not by gaining more.

cards.title: AI Tutors Jump In Too Soon
cards.hook: Put an LLM in the tutor's seat and it interrupts sooner and more often than a human would — and hands over the whole solution where a person would have offered a hint.

cards.title: Agents That Learn on the Job Without Weight Updates
cards.hook: An agent that cracks a hard request today starts from zero tomorrow. Distil each episode into a retrievable rule and a frozen model gets 2.6x better — no fine-tuning.

cards.title: LLMs Get Lost When Intent Keeps Moving
cards.hook: Real users don't state what they want up front — they reveal, revise, and redirect it mid-conversation. Rewrite existing benchmarks that way and scores drop across every model family.

cards.title: Launder the Objective, Lose the Refusal
cards.hook: Show a model a manipulative goal directly and it pushes back. Relay the same goal through two upstream agents that strip the incriminating clauses, and the model helpfully advances it.

cards.title: Skill Self-Play: Pushing the Frontier of LLM Capability with Co-Evolving Skills
cards.hook: Self-evolving models face a dilemma: verifiable environments are narrow, open-ended task generation is unreliable. This uses agent skills as the middle ground.

cards.title: Route the Task, Not the Call
cards.hook: Agent quality only reveals itself at the end of a long workflow — so a router deciding per LLM call can never tell which decision earned the reward. Decide once, at admission.

cards.title: OpenSkillRisk: Benchmarking Agent Safety with Risky Third-Party Skills
cards.hook: Give an AI agent a third-party 'skill' and even the safest setups still run unsafe actions about 17% of the time — a benchmark of 263 risky skills shows exactly how they slip through.

cards.title: Early Adoption of Agentic Coding Tools by GitHub Projects
cards.hook: 25,264 agent-written pull requests later: most open-source projects have barely touched agentic coding tools, and the ones that have still keep exactly one human gatekeeping every PR.

cards.title: Generative Compilation: On-the-Fly Compiler Feedback as AI Generates Code
cards.hook: Rust rewards AI for writing strict, safe code — and punishes it for the same reason. This lets the compiler check the model's code while it's still being written, not after.

cards.title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable, Navigable, and Editable
cards.hook: An agent is only as good as its harness — the code that builds prompts, manages state, calls tools. The real bottleneck isn't editing that code, it's finding where a behavior lives in a huge codebase.

cards.title: Hindcast: Replaying Prediction Markets to Evaluate LLM Forecasters
cards.hook: Backtesting an LLM forecaster on past events mostly measures its memory, not its foresight — because it can retrieve after-the-fact reports or was simply trained on data closer to the event.

cards.title: A Benchmark for Open-Ended Multi-Agent Coordination
cards.hook: 13 LLMs try to explore, trade, craft, and build together in an open world — and most manage only ~6% of normalized return. Communication, not raw capability, turns out to be the biggest lever.

cards.title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
cards.hook: Multi-agent LLM setups help sometimes and hurt other times, with no clear pattern — until you view them as an information bottleneck problem: compressing context helps only when it loses less than it saves.

cards.title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
cards.hook: A 3,843-trajectory autopsy of coding agents finds most failures aren't slips — they're wrong beliefs formed in the first few steps, invisible until it's too late to recover.

cards.title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench: Testing the Limits of Agents on Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks
cards.hook: 46 terminal tasks that take hours, not minutes — and today's best agent still only nails 15% of them, with the average model managing barely 4%.

cards.title: Multi-Agent LLMs Fail to Explore Each Other
cards.hook: Drop LLM agents into a room together and they don't probe each other's abilities — they lock into narrow, polarized patterns that tank coordination and inflate regret.

cards.title: What Building Shippy Taught Us About Building Agents
cards.hook: When a wrong answer can send a patrol boat miles off course, Ai2's maritime agent Shippy leans on deterministic tools and sandboxed sessions instead of hoping the model behaves.

cards.title: CompactionRL: Reinforcement Learning with Context Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
cards.hook: Long-running coding agents eventually run out of context before finishing the job. CompactionRL trains them to summarize their own history mid-task, as part of the RL objective itself.

cards.title: Vera: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale
cards.hook: Testing agent safety by hand doesn't scale — Vera automates the whole pipeline and finds a 93.9% average attack success rate across four production agent frameworks.

cards.title: Aria: Letting a Code Agent Write Its Own Formal Proofs
cards.hook: Prior LLM provers force the model into a fixed, human-designed strategy and still prove only a fraction of their targets. A free-roaming Claude Code agent, unconstrained, proves every single one.

cards.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
cards.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

cards.title: AutoMem: Automated Learning of Memory as a Cognitive Skill
cards.hook: AutoMem treats knowing what to remember and when to retrieve it — metamemory — as a trainable skill, and tuning memory alone roughly doubles to quadruples performance on long-horizon games.

cards.title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
cards.hook: PAW compiles a natural-language function spec into a small reusable adapter instead of prompting an LLM every call — matching a 32B model's quality at a fiftieth of the memory.

cards.title: Steerability via Constraints: A Substrate for Scalable Oversight of Coding Agents
cards.hook: Coding agents are already capable enough that human review is the bottleneck — this paper borrows access control and network policy from engineering-org playbooks to make oversight scale instead.

cards.title: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
cards.hook: Give an LLM agent a private, off-the-record channel during a debate, and its 'real opinion' can diverge sharply from what it says publicly — even with no explicit incentive to lie.

cards.title: Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop?
cards.hook: Across 28,000+ tasks, agents often can't tell when to quit — some never give up when they should, others bail out only after dozens of wasted tool calls.

cards.title: Scaling the Horizon, Not the Parameters
cards.hook: A 35B mixture-of-experts agent matches trillion-parameter models on long-horizon tasks — by scaling how long its trajectories run, not how big its weights are.

cards.title: Attractor States Emerge in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
cards.hook: Let two LLMs debate long enough and one model's style pulls the other toward it — Claude Haiku drags partners into its own habits, while GPT-4.1 nano is easily swayed.

cards.title: Entity Binding Failures in Tool-Augmented Agents
cards.hook: An agent can pick the right tool and still email the wrong Alex — 'entity binding' failures slip past standard tool-correctness checks in up to 26% of runs.

cards.title: OSWorld 2.0: Long-Horizon Computer Use, Stress-Tested
cards.hook: 108 realistic computer-use workflows averaging 1.6 human-hours each expose how far agents are from professional-grade computer use — the best model completes only 20.6%.

cards.title: Plans Don't Persist: Context Management Is Load-Bearing for Agents
cards.hook: An agent writes a plan, then context compression evicts it. This paper shows the plan never became internal state — once it leaves the window, the agent forgets it and task success craters.

cards.title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
cards.hook: Checking a solution used to be easier than writing one. For coding agents that's flipped — and this paper argues no fixed reward works forever: verification must co-evolve with the model.

cards.title: Computer Use in Gemini 3.5 Flash
cards.hook: DeepMind put computer-use agents — reading the screen, then clicking, typing, and scrolling through real UIs — into its fast, low-cost Flash tier.

cards.title: PlanBench-XL: Long-Horizon Planning in Large Tool Ecosystems
cards.hook: A benchmark of 1,665 tools shows top agents plan fine until tools start failing silently — then GPT-5.4's success crashes from 52% to 11%.

cards.title: Beyond Static Leaderboards for Agents
cards.hook: Topping an agent leaderboard doesn't mean it'll work when deployed: aggregate-score rankings don't transfer out-of-distribution. Rank by predictive validity instead.

cards.title: VibeThinker-3B: Frontier Reasoning in a Small Model
cards.hook: A 3B model matches giant flagships on hard math and coding - because verifiable reasoning, it turns out, compresses into a tiny 'reasoning core.'

cards.title: EvoArena: Testing Agents in Environments That Keep Changing
cards.hook: Most agent benchmarks freeze the world. EvoArena makes the environment keep updating beneath the agent — and finds today's agents crack, averaging under 40%.

cards.title: MaxProof: One Model as Generator, Verifier, Refiner, and Ranker
cards.hook: Treat one model as proof writer, checker, fixer, and judge; search a population of candidate proofs; pick a winner by tournament — enough, the authors report, to clear math-olympiad gold.

cards.title: SpatialClaw: Code as the Action Interface for Spatial Reasoning
cards.hook: Give a vision-language agent a live Python kernel instead of a fixed tool menu, and let it write one cell at a time. That flexibility lifts 3D/4D spatial reasoning by 11 points.

cards.title: Agents' Last Exam: Benchmarking Agents on Real Economic Work
cards.hook: Frontier agents ace academic benchmarks but flop on real jobs — Agents' Last Exam scores them on 1,000+ economically valuable workflows, where the hardest tier sees just a 2.6% pass rate.

cards.title: OpenAI o3: Reasoning that Uses Tools
cards.hook: o3 is the first reasoning model that can agentically reach for every ChatGPT tool mid-thought - web search, Python on your files, image input, image generation - and combine them to solve a problem.

cards.title: Large Language Models Are Zero-Shot Reasoners
cards.hook: Appending 'Let's think step by step' to a prompt unlocks multi-step reasoning with zero examples - chain-of-thought without the example-writing overhead.

cards.title: ReAct: Reasoning + Acting
cards.hook: Thinking alone can drift; acting alone is blind. ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls so an LLM can plan, look things up, and correct course — the template for agents.

cards.title: Toolformer: Language Models That Use Tools
cards.hook: Instead of hand-scripting when to call a calculator or search, Toolformer lets the model teach itself — try API calls during training, keep the ones that actually help.

cards.title: Ignorance or Incompetence? Building Agent Tasks That Tell the Difference
cards.hook: When an agent fails a professional task, was it incapable or just missing a convention nobody published? This protocol splits the instruction from the private knowledge so you can test which.

cards.title: Paint What You See: A Benchmark for Dexterous Visual Tool Use
cards.hook: Ask a multimodal agent to repaint a reference image stroke by stroke and it stalls at roughly half-right — then gets worse the longer it works.

cards.title: Naive Prompt Optimization Beats the Fancy Search
cards.hook: Prompt optimizers have grown elaborate search machinery. A single-lineage loop that just asks a teacher model to revise the prompt matches or beats GEPA with fewer rollouts.

cards.title: Ladders in Chaos: Sequential Beats Parallel Test-Time Scaling — Up to a Point
cards.hook: Revising your own answer beats sampling many independent ones, in translation at least. But push the budget too far and fluency keeps rising while accuracy starts slipping.

cards.title: WikiSkill: Give the Agent a Wiki, Not Just Skills
cards.hook: Auto-discovered agent skills work, but the insight behind them gets lost. WikiSkill keeps a persistent wiki alongside the skills — and skills borrowed from other models beat self-evolved ones.

cards.title: AnTrap: Are Android GUI Agents Robust Against Runtime Anomalies?
cards.hook: Real phones throw pop-ups, misfired taps, and dead-end screens at you. Inject those into GUI agent runs and all 16 leading models degrade — some in ways adversarial training can't fix.

cards.title: AsymSpec: Context-Asymmetric Speculative Decoding for Agentic LLMs
cards.hook: Speculative decoding assumes drafter and verifier read the same context. Let the small drafter see everything while the big model reads a compressed view, and compression stops costing accuracy.

cards.title: Code World Model: Coding Agent as World Brain
cards.hook: Video world models learn what happens, not why. Put a coding agent in charge of the rules — writing executable code that holds world state — and let the video model handle only the pixels.

cards.title: JIT-Agent: Scaling Harness Intelligence via Just-in-Time Harness Evolution
cards.hook: If the harness matters as much as the model, why is it still hand-written? JIT-Agent trains a model whose whole job is to synthesize a fresh harness for whatever task shows up.

cards.title: MARS: Hand the Problem to the Right Specialist
cards.hook: Most multi-agent coding pipelines split work into planner, coder, debugger. MARS splits it by algorithmic topic instead — and gets most of the accuracy of a heavier pipeline at a third of the wall-clock cost.

cards.title: MobilePA-Bench: Phone Agents in a Live Sandbox
cards.hook: GUI benchmarks test tapping; function-call benchmarks test string matching. This one runs a real phone sandbox with live app databases — and frontier models get brittle fast.

cards.title: SwarmWorld: Stigmergic Technological Evolution in Societies of LLM Agents
cards.hook: Drop identical LLM agents into a shared world with no roles and no recipes. They differentiate, build on each other's leftovers, and accumulate technology — mostly by looking, not talking.

cards.title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling
cards.hook: Recurrent depth helps most where tool use is actually hard: chaining calls, holding intermediate state, keeping dependencies straight. Single API calls barely notice.

cards.title: AgentRewind: Give Agents an Undo Button
cards.hook: Most agent research tries to prevent mistakes. AgentRewind asks what happens after one — checkpoint the context and the environment together, so the agent can rewind and retry with what it learned.

cards.title: Agent Memory: Consolidate by Segment, Not by Turn
cards.hook: Most agent memory systems call an LLM after every exchange, so memory gets more expensive as the conversation grows. Batching into semantic segments cut construction tokens by 86%.

cards.title: Second Thought: Reasoning in Parallel While an Agent Acts
cards.hook: Every time a ReAct agent calls a tool and waits, its reasoning sits idle. Second Thought fills that gap with side branches that think ahead — no retraining, fewer turns.

cards.title: Spatial Memory Agent: Self-Improvement Without Touching the Weights
cards.hook: A frozen VLM gets better at spatial reasoning by writing itself notes — verified lessons, scored by how well they transfer, retrieved at inference time.

cards.title: Wrong but Useful: Bad Answers That Still Help
cards.hook: Multi-agent systems filter messages by how likely they are to be correct. But a wrong answer can carry a good decomposition — and in every model and benchmark tested, wrong-helpful messages showed up.

cards.title: Open Coding Agents Are Overfitting to Their Harness
cards.hook: Almost all open agent trajectory data is collected under OpenHands. Models fine-tuned on it score well there and fall apart under any other scaffold — a gap the base models don't have.

cards.title: Macaron-V1: Mixture-of-LoRA for Continual Learning
cards.hook: Freeze the base model, keep a shelf of specialist LoRA adapters, pick one per user turn. It's a bet that continual learning belongs in the adapters, not the weights.

cards.title: Can LLM Agents Stick to the Script? A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Consistency in Interactive Narratives
cards.hook: Fluent writing is not the same as staying consistent: the best model keeps its story straight for only 42% of runs past 20 turns of adversarial play.

cards.title: Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution
cards.hook: Instead of keeping the agent alive across a long project, keep the project alive and let agents be disposable — enough to grow a 250k-line Rust C compiler for $44.

cards.title: SHAPER: Adapting Embodied Agents by Evolving Skills and Harness, Not Weights
cards.hook: When a robot agent fails in a new environment, the reflex is to fine-tune. SHAPER freezes the model and instead evolves the skills and harness wrapped around it — no data, no rewards, no training run.

cards.title: Spark-to-Paper: Research Paper Generation as Composable Skills
cards.hook: Not a new agent platform — thirteen skills bolted into an existing coding assistant, with integrity checks deciding which claims survive contact with the experiments.

cards.title: ToolHazard: Synthesizing Adversarial Environments for Agent Security
cards.hook: Prompt-injection benchmarks are hand-built, so they cover the domains someone had time to write. ToolHazard generates the environments — and the attacks inside them — instead.

cards.title: IDEAgent: Quality-Diversity Search for Research Ideas
cards.hook: Idea generators optimize for quality or for diversity, and get either near-clones or piles of nonsense. Treating ideation as a joint search changes the objective.

cards.title: Molt: A PyTorch-Native Training Framework for Agentic RL
cards.hook: NVIDIA's bet: an agentic RL codebase small enough for a researcher — or a coding assistant — to hold in their head entirely, without giving up performance.

cards.title: Don't Resample — Rewind to the Bad Token
cards.hook: Resampling after a failure throws away the reasoning that was still correct. TTEL finds the token where things went wrong and branches from there — same pass@64, half the tokens.

cards.title: DocOps: Benchmarking Agents That Edit Real Documents
cards.hook: Even frontier agents can't reliably edit complex documents: a verifiable benchmark pins the failures on three modes — state-tracking collapse, shallow verification, and destructive metadata edits.

cards.title: The Ethics of Autonomous AI Agents for Offensive Security
cards.hook: Autonomous AI agents drop the skill floor for cyberattacks and blur who's to blame. This paper maps three kinds of 'indeterminacy' that break existing dual-use ethics frameworks.

cards.title: Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions?
cards.hook: Let an LLM write itself 'notes to self' — reusable strategies distilled from its own solution attempts — and its math and logic reasoning improves, with self-written notes as good as a teacher's.

cards.title: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation
cards.hook: Most agent-optimization papers report a one-shot gain and stop. Rerun the optimizer on new tasks and two of three popular methods actually make the agent worse than doing nothing.

cards.title: How Agents Ask for Permission: User Permissions for AI Agents
cards.hook: Most agent-security work assumes one policy fits every user. This survey of 21 proposals plus five commercial agents finds user-level permission handling is still full of gaps.

cards.title: From Human-Centric to Agentic Code Review: The Impact of Different Generations of Generative AI Technology on Review Quality
cards.hook: 1.02 million pull requests tracked across three code-review eras find AI reviewers speed up decisions — but faster isn't better: review quality doesn't improve alongside it.

cards.title: Chain of Thought Is a Scaling Trap? The Case for Latent Reasoning
cards.hook: A visible chain of thought reads like the model's thinking — but it can be an unfaithful, expensive trace. The next wave reasons in hidden state instead of tokens.

cards.title: KnowAct-GUIClaw: Know Deeply, Act Perfectly, Personal GUI Assistant with Self-Evolving Memory and Skill
cards.hook: A GUI agent framework that treats every finished task as a lesson: it banks the experience into memory and skills, then reuses them across Android, iOS, HarmonyOS, and Windows.

cards.title: RESOURCE2SKILL: Distilling Executable Agent Skills from Human-Created Multimodal Resources
cards.hook: Most agent skill libraries are hand-written text. This framework mines skills straight out of the tutorial videos, repos, and articles humans already made for each other.

cards.title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
cards.hook: Search agents forget what they've already tried and loop on failed queries, burning their budget. SearchOS gives them a shared, persistent memory of what's been searched, found, and failed.

cards.title: Interaction Scaling: Grounding the Third Axis of Test-Time Compute
cards.hook: Reasoning longer and sampling more both mine the same frozen weights — they can't tell a model anything new. Let it poke a real tool instead, and a coding loop hits 100% pass rate with zero variance.

cards.title: Is Agentic Code Review Helpful? Mining Developers' Feedback to CodeRabbit Reviews in the Wild
cards.hook: CodeRabbit leaves review comments on hundreds of thousands of real pull requests. A large-scale study of how developers actually respond finds more than half get rejected outright.

cards.title: Danus: Orchestrating Mathematical Reasoning Agents with Fact-Graph Memory
cards.hook: Parallel proof-search agents can generate claims faster than anyone can keep straight. Danus fixes that with a shared fact graph that only admits claims a stateless verifier has checked.

cards.title: LingBot-World 2.0: An Agent-Piloted Infinite World Model
cards.hook: Interactive world models usually run out of road — quality degrades, or the action set stays thin. LingBot-World 2.0 stays coherent forever and puts an agent inside to invent what's next.

cards.title: ResearchStudio-Reel: One Extraction, Three Editable Outputs From a Paper
cards.hook: Turning a paper into a poster, talk video, and blog is usually done by hand, three times over. ResearchStudio-Reel extracts it once and generates all three — beating even authors' own posters.

cards.title: Spider 2.0-AIFunc: Extending Real-World Text-to-SQL to AI-Native SQL Workflows
cards.hook: Cloud platforms let analysts call AI functions right inside SQL. Spider 2.0-AIFunc is the first benchmark testing whether models can write that kind of query — top models still cap out near 70%.

cards.title: SPORK: Self-Speculative Forking to Accelerate Agentic LLM Inference
cards.hook: An agent's tool-call loop idles the GPU 16-37% of the time waiting on results. SPORK has the model predict its own next tool call early enough to start it before reasoning even finishes.

cards.title: UI-MOPD: Teaching One GUI Agent Many Platforms Without Forgetting
cards.hook: Train a GUI agent on a new platform and it often forgets the old ones. UI-MOPD picks a different teacher per platform on the fly, so cross-platform learning stops fighting itself.

cards.title: WebSwarm: Recursive Multi-Agent Orchestration for Deep-and-Wide Web Search
cards.hook: One long search trajectory can't be both deep and wide at once. WebSwarm lets the search tree grow instead: any node that can't solve its own piece just spawns children and waits for their evidence.

cards.title: Agentic Test-Time Training: Adapting Mid-Episode
cards.hook: LLM agents degrade over long episodes, repeating failed moves — this method updates the model's weights continuously during the episode itself, but only on genuinely new information.

cards.title: Doomed from the Start: Predicting Agent Failure Before It Happens
cards.hook: An agent that's going to fail often shows it in its hidden activations from round one — long before its actual behavior looks any different. Reading that signal saves nearly half the compute.

cards.title: EdgeBench: Scaling Laws for Learning from Real Environments
cards.hook: Pretraining has scaling laws everyone knows by heart. This paper finds the first one for what happens after deployment — how fast agents actually improve from real-world experience.

cards.title: NVIDIA Opens 10T Tokens of Synthetic Data for Agentic AI
cards.hook: Real agent behavior needs data on tool failures and recovery paths that companies rarely want to share — NVIDIA's answer is 10+ trillion tokens of synthetic data built to stand in for it.

cards.title: Untrusted Content Masking: A Trust Boundary for Web Agents
cards.hook: Provable prompt-injection defenses rely on never letting an agent read untrusted content directly. Web agents break that just by looking at the page — this restores it via the page's own structure.

cards.title: AutoTrainess: Teaching Language Models to Improve Language Models Autonomously
cards.hook: Training a model is more than writing code — AutoTrainess gives agents purpose-built interfaces for planning, data prep, and training runs, and clearly out-trains agents left in a raw CLI.

cards.title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
cards.hook: Full agentic evals like SWE-Bench and GAIA can cost thousands of dollars and days to run — PACE predicts those scores from a tiny, cheap subset of ordinary benchmarks, at under 1% of the cost.

cards.title: TUA-Bench: Benchmarking General-Purpose Terminal Agents
cards.hook: 120 real terminal tasks — from email triage to PhD-level scientific workflows — show even Claude Opus 4.8 tops out around 66%, far from reliable general computer use.

cards.title: Critique of Agent Model: Agentic vs. Agentive Systems
cards.hook: When is a system really an 'agent' and not just a clever workflow? This paper draws the line at whether agency is internalized or scaffolded — and sketches an architecture for the former.

cards.title: GUI vs. CLI: Where Computer-Use Agents Get Stuck
cards.hook: Should an agent click buttons or type commands? A matched benchmark giving both the same 440 tasks finds GUI agents win by default — but CLI agents leap ahead once their skill library is filled in.

cards.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI
cards.hook: A practitioner reference that walks the whole agent stack — transformer substrate, RLHF, memory, MCP, A2A, multi-agent topologies — on the thesis that good agents demand understanding every layer.

cards.title: DataClaw0: Data Refinement as a Learnable Skill
cards.hook: Instead of scrubbing data with fixed rules, what if an agent learned to tailor it? DataClaw0 turns data refinement into a trainable skill judged by how well models train on its output.

cards.title: OpenRath: Sessions as First-Class Agent State
cards.hook: Agent state is usually scattered across logs you stitch back together. OpenRath makes the Session a first-class value you can fork, replay, and inspect like a tensor.

cards.title: Playful Agentic Robot Learning
cards.hook: Let a robot play before it works: it invents its own exploratory tasks and distills the wins into a reusable skill library — and the skills transfer to other agents for free.

cards.title: QUEST: An Open Deep-Research Agent
cards.hook: A fully open Deep Research agent trained on ~32 H100s and ~8K synthetic samples — recipe, code, weights, and data all released, and reportedly competitive with frontier closed systems.

cards.title: FORT-Searcher: Shortcut-Resistant Tasks for Search Agents
cards.hook: Harder-looking questions aren't harder to search. FORT builds tasks where the intended search can't collapse into a cheap shortcut — and trains better deep-search agents on them.

cards.title: Why One Engineer Dropped Embeddings for BM25 in Tool Selection
cards.hook: An engineer running an agent with ~140 tools dropped embedding-based tool selection for plain BM25 — cosine similarity over short tool descriptions was dangerous in production.

cards.title: Token Budgets: When Agents Burn Money
cards.hook: A single retry loop can spend thousands of dollars before anyone notices. This paper catalogs 63 real budget-overrun incidents — and asks the type system to make over-spending a compile error.

cards.title: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol
cards.hook: A2A is an open standard for agents from different vendors to discover and delegate to each other — the agent-to-agent complement to MCP's agent-to-tool layer.

cards.title: Claude Agent Skills
cards.hook: Agent Skills package instructions, scripts, and resources into folders an agent loads on demand — composable, portable expertise, later opened as a standard like MCP.

cards.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
cards.hook: Sample the model many times, let each run reason its own way, then take the majority answer - diverse reasoning paths vote out individual errors.

cards.title: Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong
cards.hook: Five world-model RL agents can master Atari Pong on paper — but freeze their world models and watch closely: the ball vanishes, bounces wrong, or phases through the paddle.

cards.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
cards.hook: DeepSeek shows strong reasoning can emerge from RL on verifiable rewards with minimal supervised data - and those reasoning traces can be distilled into smaller models.

cards.title: TRACE: Turn-Level Reward Assignment via Credit Estimation for Long-Horizon Agents
cards.hook: A failed agent rollout might still contain dozens of genuinely useful actions — outcome-only RL punishes every one of them the same as the final mistake. TRACE assigns credit per tool call instead, with no extra critic.

cards.title: Catching Agent Memory Poisoning from Tool-Call Logs Alone
cards.hook: A memory-poisoning attack on an LLM agent leaves a near-perfect fingerprint in its tool-call order — a simple rule catches it at AUC 0.956, a small classifier pushes that to 0.99.

cards.title: Your Parser Already Knows Which Tokens Matter
cards.hook: Constrained decoding tracks grammar state to keep JSON valid. PASK reuses that same signal to decide what to keep in the KV cache — and a wrong field is a failed tool call, not a stylistic blemish.

cards.title: SLPO: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoners That Think in Vectors
cards.hook: Latent reasoners think in continuous vectors, not tokens — but couldn't learn from outcome rewards the way chain-of-thought models can. SLPO gives them a surrogate policy so RL finally works.

cards.title: Partially Correlated Verifier Cascades: Concave Log-Odds and Blind-Spot Ceilings
cards.hook: Chain enough independent verifier checks and failure should vanish exponentially. In practice, treating correlated verifiers as independent underestimates failure by 20x at 5 checks — and 3000x at 10.

cards.title: SEED: Self-Evolving On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
cards.hook: Outcome-only RL tells an agent whether an episode succeeded, not which step mattered. SEED has the policy mine its own trajectories for hindsight lessons, then distills them back in as dense, token-level signal.

cards.title: Latent Memory Palace: Reasoning for Control as Autoregressive Variational Inference
cards.hook: LLMs can choose to think longer on hard questions. This paper gets robot control policies to do the same — allocating adaptive test-time compute in a latent 'memory palace' instead of language.

cards.title: OPID: On-Policy Skill Distillation for Agentic RL
cards.hook: Outcome-only RL tells an agent it failed but not which move was the mistake. OPID mines that lesson from the agent's own finished trajectories — turning hindsight into dense, per-token supervision.

cards.title: Economy of Minds: Agents That Bid to Act
cards.hook: Skip the orchestrator. Let agents bid in auctions for the right to act, pay each other, and accumulate wealth — and collective intelligence emerges from the market, not from central control.

cards.title: World Models Meet Language Models
cards.hook: A world model can imagine what happens next; an LLM can reason about it. The hard part is knowing when to trust the daydream — and when the simulation is just plausible nonsense.

cards.title: Stop Anthropomorphizing Intermediate Tokens
cards.hook: Calling the scratchpad 'thinking' imports an assumption. A model's intermediate tokens augment its own prompt — which is why the answer can be right while the 'reasoning' rambles.

cards.title: OpenAI o1: Learning to Reason with Reinforcement Learning
cards.hook: OpenAI's o1 lets a model think via a long internal chain-of-thought before answering - spending more compute at inference time visibly improves reasoning.

cards.title: Harness-1: RL for Search Agents with State-Externalizing Harnesses
cards.hook: Stop making the policy remember everything. Harness-1 moves a search agent's bookkeeping into the environment, so RL only has to learn the decisions that matter.

cards.title: Prompt Injection Defenses Fall Apart in Long Context
cards.hook: Injection benchmarks are all short-context, which has been flattering the defenses. Stretch the input to tens of thousands of tokens and even naive attacks walk through state-of-the-art protections.

cards.title: Sliding Window Beats Linear Attention
cards.hook: The cheap baseline nobody bothered to run wins: sliding-window attention with sinks matches or beats retrofitted linear-attention models, and needs no post-training at all.

cards.title: Agent Memory Poisoning Beats Content Screening
cards.hook: Poison 1.2% of an agent's long-term memory with plain false sentences and accuracy falls from 0.85 to 0.30 — while an injection screener catches literally none of them.

cards.title: Agent Memory Is a Dose, Not a Switch
cards.hook: IBM Research tested how much extracted guideline memory to give an agent. The right amount depends on the model: strong ones absorb everything, weaker ones do better with curated retrieval.

cards.title: The Information Abundance Paradox: Long Context Can Undermine What a Model Knows
cards.hook: If the answer is always in the context window, the model stops bothering to learn it. Past an intermediate context length, more training context makes a model weaker without its crutch.

cards.title: Referential Dangling: How Prompt Compression Quietly Breaks Multi-Hop Answers
cards.hook: Compressors score chunks independently, so they can keep the sentence holding the answer and delete the one defining who it's about — leaving text that reads fine and answers wrong.

cards.title: Agents That Learn on the Job Without Weight Updates
cards.hook: An agent that cracks a hard request today starts from zero tomorrow. Distil each episode into a retrievable rule and a frozen model gets 2.6x better — no fine-tuning.

cards.title: CompactionRL: Reinforcement Learning with Context Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
cards.hook: Long-running coding agents eventually run out of context before finishing the job. CompactionRL trains them to summarize their own history mid-task, as part of the RL objective itself.

cards.title: Why Long-Context Speed Comes Down to Prefill and KV Heads
cards.hook: Everyone benchmarks token-generation speed. A community test of 13 models at 65K-128K context found that's the wrong number — prefill dominates, and KV head count beats parameter count.

cards.title: AutoMem: Automated Learning of Memory as a Cognitive Skill
cards.hook: AutoMem treats knowing what to remember and when to retrieve it — metamemory — as a trainable skill, and tuning memory alone roughly doubles to quadruples performance on long-horizon games.

cards.title: Plans Don't Persist: Context Management Is Load-Bearing for Agents
cards.hook: An agent writes a plan, then context compression evicts it. This paper shows the plan never became internal state — once it leaves the window, the agent forgets it and task success craters.

cards.title: MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA)
cards.hook: Quadratic attention chokes at a million tokens. MiniMax runs exact attention over only a Top-k of key-value blocks per query group — cutting per-token attention compute ~28x at 1M context.

cards.title: The KV Cache & Continuous Batching
cards.hook: Generating one token reuses every prior key and value - that growing cache is why LLM inference is memory-bound, and continuous batching is how servers fight back.

cards.title: FlashAttention: Fast, Memory-Efficient Exact Attention
cards.hook: Attention got faster not by approximating it, but by being smarter about GPU memory — never writing the giant attention matrix out to slow memory.

cards.title: Funes: Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own
cards.hook: Your agent's reasoning from last Tuesday vanishes when the session ends. Funes indexes past sessions locally so an agent can recall its own prior decisions instead of being re-briefed.

cards.title: What an Engram Actually Is
cards.hook: The n-gram tables in new open models are not a trick for running 1T parameters off an SSD — they are an embedding table with a longer key, and that is a more interesting idea.

cards.title: Agent Memory: Consolidate by Segment, Not by Turn
cards.hook: Most agent memory systems call an LLM after every exchange, so memory gets more expensive as the conversation grows. Batching into semantic segments cut construction tokens by 86%.

cards.title: Chain of Thought Is a Scaling Trap? The Case for Latent Reasoning
cards.hook: A visible chain of thought reads like the model's thinking — but it can be an unfaithful, expensive trace. The next wave reasons in hidden state instead of tokens.

cards.title: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies
cards.hook: Robot policies mostly look at the last step or two. NVIDIA's RoboTTT pushes visuomotor context to 8,000 timesteps without slowing inference — and finds performance keeps climbing the whole way.

cards.title: WILDTRACE: Benchmarking Natural Evidence Trails in Long-Context Reasoning
cards.hook: Most long-context tests plant a fake 'needle' in a haystack. Real evidence doesn't look like that — passing needle tests may not mean a model can truly reason over a document.

cards.title: HiLS Attention: Learning Chunk Selection for Near-Infinite Context
cards.hook: Sparse attention never quite matched full attention because chunk selection was a heuristic. This version trains chunk selection end-to-end — then extrapolates 64x past its training length.

cards.title: When Claws Remember but Do Not Tell: Stealthy Memory Injection
cards.hook: One poisoned email is enough: this attack tricks a persistent personal agent into silently writing false memories, hiding the evidence from the user, and acting on the lie later.

cards.title: MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory
cards.hook: Agent memory sounds purely good — until retrieved memories start pushing an agent to agree with the user over the facts. MemSyco-Bench is built specifically to catch that failure.

cards.title: Language Models Need Sleep
cards.hook: Humans consolidate the day's memories while sleeping. This paper gives LLMs a 'sleep' phase to distill fragile short-term context into stable long-term weights — and a 'dreaming' phase to rehearse.

cards.title: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
cards.hook: Most tokens only need to look at their neighbors, so swap full attention for a sliding window plus a few global tokens and the cost goes from quadratic to linear in sequence length.

cards.title: A Hobbyist CUDA Kernel Brings DeepSeek-V4 Flash's Full 1M Context to One GPU
cards.hook: Missing CUDA support for DeepSeek-V4 Flash's sparse-attention indexer meant llama.cpp needed ~256GB of VRAM for 1M-token context. One contributor's kernel patch shrinks that to a single RTX 5090.

cards.title: CRISP: Reading the Sparse-Attention Routing Decision Straight Off the Attention Map
cards.hook: Long-context prefill is quadratic, so servers route attention heads to sparse patterns. CRISP shows the routing decision is already readable off the attention map's structure.

cards.title: KV Cache Eviction, Formalized
cards.hook: Everyone drops KV cache entries with clever heuristics. Formalize the problem properly and it turns into expectation estimation — which finally lets you correct for what you threw away.

cards.title: T^2MLR: Transformer with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence
cards.hook: Decoding squeezes a transformer's thinking through token space each step. T2MLR pipes a cached middle-layer state into the next pass — recurring 20% of the network often beats looping it all.

cards.title: Latent Context Language Models: Compressing the Prompt, Not the Cache
cards.hook: Instead of shrinking the KV cache, compress the prompt itself: a small encoder folds a long context into a few latent embeddings that a bigger decoder reads — letting agents skim and expand on demand.

cards.title: RoPE: Rotary Position Embedding
cards.hook: Encode position by rotating query/key vectors - relative distances then fall out of the dot product for free, no extra tokens or additive embeddings needed.

cards.title: Sigmoid Attention Makes KV Eviction Stick
cards.hook: Learned cache-eviction gates train softly but must delete hard at inference. Swap softmax for sigmoid attention and that jump stops hurting — even though sigmoid is the worse LM.

cards.title: FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context Serving
cards.hook: Prefill is where long-context inference burns its compute. This turns a sparse-attention prototype into a production backend — and reports up to 47x over FlashAttention-2 at 128K.

cards.title: Top-k KV Eviction Can't Know What It Threw Away
cards.hook: Deterministic cache eviction is blind by construction: nothing you kept reveals how much error the deletions caused. Sample randomly instead and the leftovers become a statistical certificate.

cards.title: The Draft Isn't Free at a Million Tokens
cards.hook: Speculative decoding assumes the draft is cheap. At million-token context the draft head reads the entire KV cache every step — and can end up slower than no speculation at all.

cards.title: Block-GTQ: RoPE-Aware Bit Allocation for KV-Cache Quantization
cards.hook: Most KV-cache quantizers spend bits evenly across a key. Block-GTQ shows that under RoPE some frequency blocks matter far more — and gives them more bits, hitting near-fp16 quality at 2–3 bits.

cards.title: Attention Amnesia: When Chain-of-Thought Tuning Breaks Long-Range Recall
cards.hook: Fine-tuning a hybrid LLM on chain-of-thought makes it reason better but quietly forget how to find a needle in a long haystack — and the fix is to just copy back two weight matrices.

cards.title: Ring Attention for Near-Infinite Context
cards.hook: Spread one long sequence across many devices and compute attention blockwise - the context length you can handle grows with the number of devices, all with exact attention and no extra overhead.

cards.title: Prefix Sliding for Efficient Test-Time Scaling
cards.hook: Most intermediate reasoning tokens stop mattering as the model reasons on. Keep only the prefix and the last few thousand tokens and you cap memory forever — 3x faster with no training.

cards.title: Extending Context Windows via Positional Interpolation
cards.hook: Don't extrapolate to positions the model never saw - squeeze the position indices back inside the trained range, and a short fine-tune stretches the context window many times over.

cards.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
cards.hook: Why retrain billions of weights when you can freeze them all and train tiny add-on matrices instead? LoRA tunes under ~1% of the parameters with near-full-fine-tune quality.

cards.title: SWE-Prime: 10% of the Trajectories, Better Results
cards.hook: A successful agent trajectory can still be full of wasted and risky steps. Filter down to the best 10% and fine-tuning beats training on everything that worked.

cards.title: How Many Bits Can a LoRA Adapter Write?
cards.hook: Everyone treats a LoRA adapter as a skill, not a record of its training data. Weighed in bits, it stores a couple per trainable parameter — and where you put them matters more than how many.

cards.title: FLAN: Instruction Tuning
cards.hook: Teach a model to follow many tasks phrased as plain instructions, and it learns to follow instructions for tasks it never saw — zero-shot.

cards.title: QLoRA: Fine-tuning Quantized LLMs
cards.hook: Fine-tune a model with tens of billions of parameters on a single GPU. QLoRA squeezes the frozen base to 4-bit, then trains LoRA adapters on top — without losing quality.

cards.title: 100 GRPO Steps to Make a 350M Model Respect Your Schema
cards.hook: Small models are cheap but sloppy about output format. Three simple programmatic rewards and about 500 samples nearly doubled a 350M model's JSON pass rate.

cards.title: Macaron-V1: Mixture-of-LoRA for Continual Learning
cards.hook: Freeze the base model, keep a shelf of specialist LoRA adapters, pick one per user turn. It's a bet that continual learning belongs in the adapters, not the weights.

cards.title: Not Every LoRA Matrix Is Worth Updating
cards.hook: LoRA trains every matrix equally hard. A matrix's condition number reveals which ones actually drive adaptation — tune the top half and you keep the accuracy for half the parameters.

cards.title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning (Adapters)
cards.hook: Don't fine-tune the whole model for every new task — slip in a few tiny trainable modules and freeze the rest. This 2019 idea seeded parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

cards.title: A Spectral Threshold That Predicts When LoRA Will Forget
cards.hook: LoRA sometimes injects 'intruder dimensions' that trigger catastrophic forgetting. This paper predicts the per-layer update strength where they appear, from the pretrained spectrum alone.

cards.title: Three Ways to Fuse Domain Experts, Compared
cards.hook: Merge task vectors, pool the RL data, or distil from multiple teachers? Average scores differ by 1.4 points — but on a single benchmark the gap hits 8.6.

cards.title: How Much Rank Does LoRA Need? Rank-Error Bounds for Transformer Attention
cards.hook: Picking a LoRA rank is normally guesswork. This paper derives what error each rank can actually achieve for attention — and shows softmax saturation means you often need less rank than you'd think.

cards.title: Scaling Laws for Hypernetwork-Based Knowledge Injection
cards.hook: Instead of fine-tuning to memorize facts, train a hypernetwork to generate a LoRA adapter that injects them — and it follows clean scaling laws with steeper out-of-distribution gains.

cards.title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: SFT, RL, and OPD Shape Calibration Differently
cards.hook: SFT, RL, and on-policy distillation all boost reasoning accuracy — but they leave completely different fingerprints on when a model's confidence signal can actually be trusted.

cards.title: SRM-LoRA: Steering LoRA's Gradients Away from Hallucination-Prone Directions
cards.hook: Most LoRA variants just shrink how many parameters you tune. SRM-LoRA changes which directions get updated at all — using geometry to steer fine-tuning away from directions tied to hallucination.

cards.title: Super Weights Are Critical to Read — But Useless to Train Alone
cards.hook: A handful of parameters wreck accuracy if removed. You'd think training just those would be the cheapest fine-tune ever. It isn't — it collapses the model to random guessing instead.

cards.title: Why QLoRA's 2e-4 Default Learning Rate Overfits Small Datasets
cards.hook: Every QLoRA tutorial says start at 2e-4. That number comes from Alpaca's 52k samples — and on the 5-10k-sample datasets most people actually fine-tune on, it can overfit before epoch one ends.

cards.title: InstructGPT: Aligning LMs with Human Feedback (RLHF)
cards.hook: A smaller model people actually like beats a bigger one they don't. InstructGPT used human preferences to make a model follow instructions — the recipe behind ChatGPT.

cards.title: Is Next-Chunk Reasoning RL Really Better Than SFT?
cards.hook: A controlled rerun finds the simplest baseline wins: plain mixed supervised fine-tuning beats next-chunk reasoning RL on no-CoT data, at over 60x less training compute.

cards.title: Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning from a Diverse Cohort
cards.hook: Self-rewarding RL collapses because a model's errors reinforce themselves. Co-RL breaks the loop by having a diverse cohort of models grade each other — no labels at all.

cards.title: Why Multi-Task SFT Fights Itself and Multi-Task RL Doesn't
cards.hook: Train a model on several tasks with SFT and they interfere; with RL they coexist. The difference is a bound: SFT interference scales with gradient magnitude, RL's only with variance.

cards.title: DynamicRubric: Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies
cards.hook: As a model improves, its candidate answers get so close in quality that the reward model can't tell them apart. DynamicRubric fixes the bottleneck by evolving the evaluator alongside the policy.

cards.title: Multimodal Reward Hacking: RL Creates It, Doesn't Just Inherit It
cards.hook: Train a multimodal model with outcome-only RL rewards and it doesn't just exploit shortcuts it already had — the training itself manufactures new ones, up to 48% of the time.

cards.title: Constitutional AI
cards.hook: What if a model could critique and improve its own answers against a written set of principles, instead of relying on humans to label every harmful case?

cards.title: Proper Scoring Rules Are Not Interchangeable as Training Objectives
cards.hook: Five scoring rules that all reward honest probabilities in theory produced five differently-behaved forecasters in practice — same accuracy, different shape of error.

cards.title: V-Rubrics: Grading a VLM's Answer Fact by Fact
cards.hook: A single ungrounded object or misread chart value can sink an otherwise good answer — and a pass/fail reward can't tell you which part broke. V-Rubrics hands out partial credit per visual claim.

cards.title: "This Is Not a Course. It Is a Journey."
cards.hook: That tic has a name Cicero knew: epanorthosis. This essay argues LLMs overuse it because their training text is full of promotional prose and RLHF rewards emphatic phrasing.

cards.title: Molt: A PyTorch-Native Training Framework for Agentic RL
cards.hook: NVIDIA's bet: an agentic RL codebase small enough for a researcher — or a coding assistant — to hold in their head entirely, without giving up performance.

cards.title: Qwen-Image-2.0-RL: RLHF for a Diffusion Model
cards.hook: Qwen's team applied RLHF and on-policy distillation to a text-to-image diffusion model — the same post-training playbook that shaped chat models, now tuning image generation and editing.

cards.title: RL Teaches LLMs to Translate Languages They've Never Seen
cards.hook: Instead of memorizing a new language, what if a model learned the meta-skill of reading a grammar book on the fly? RL with a crude string-overlap reward gets it there.

cards.title: Evolution Strategies Beat GRPO on Reasoning Coverage
cards.hook: GRPO sharpens one answer and collapses entropy. Evolution strategies keep the population diverse — improving pass@1 while also raising pass@k, which GRPO gives up.

cards.title: TTPO: Training at Test Time Without Labels
cards.hook: Majority voting is a fragile teacher — one bad vote poisons every token. TTPO exploits an asymmetry: rollouts that disagree with the vote are usually wrong even when the vote is too.

cards.title: Annotations as Rollouts: Cheaper RL for Video Models
cards.hook: RL post-training wastes most of its samples on bad rollouts. OraRL drops the ground-truth annotation into the group as an oracle rollout — and has to fix the advantage math to make it work.

cards.title: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
cards.hook: RL post-training is usually studied apart from pretraining. Using chess as a testbed, this paper shows post-RL performance is predictable from pretraining loss alone.

cards.title: TRACE: Turn-Level Reward Assignment via Credit Estimation for Long-Horizon Agents
cards.hook: A failed agent rollout might still contain dozens of genuinely useful actions — outcome-only RL punishes every one of them the same as the final mistake. TRACE assigns credit per tool call instead, with no extra critic.

cards.title: Pessimism's Paradox: Conservative Training Can Backfire
cards.hook: Staying close to safe, well-supported behavior during offline training is supposed to prevent reward hacking later — this paper finds the opposite: more conservatism, more hacking.

cards.title: Beyond Scalar Rewards: Reward as a Score Distribution
cards.hook: Human taste isn't a single number. Z-Reward models visual preference as a distribution over rubric scores, then distills that reasoning judge into a small one needing no reasoning at inference.

cards.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
cards.hook: RLHF works but is fiddly: a separate reward model and a finicky RL loop. DPO reaches the same goal with one simple loss — and became a popular default.

cards.title: PPO: Proximal Policy Optimization
cards.hook: Reinforcement learning is notoriously unstable. PPO's fix is simple: never let a single update move the policy too far. That restraint made it the field's workhorse.

cards.title: Three Ways to Fuse Domain Experts, Compared
cards.hook: Merge task vectors, pool the RL data, or distil from multiple teachers? Average scores differ by 1.4 points — but on a single benchmark the gap hits 8.6.

cards.title: Use a Weak Model to Stop Your Strong One Getting Stuck
cards.hook: RLVR collapses a model's entropy until it only knows one way to think. Feeding it half-finished reasoning from a smaller, worse model breaks the rut — no reward engineering required.

cards.title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
cards.hook: Instead of copying a teacher's raw outputs, this method distills only the *change* reasoning-tuning made — a sharper signal that beats standard on-policy distillation across math, science, and code.

cards.title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: SFT, RL, and OPD Shape Calibration Differently
cards.hook: SFT, RL, and on-policy distillation all boost reasoning accuracy — but they leave completely different fingerprints on when a model's confidence signal can actually be trusted.

cards.title: Importance Ratios Mean Different Things at Different Entropies
cards.hook: Async RL clips stale tokens by how big their importance ratio is. But the ratio's natural scale tracks token entropy — so one threshold admits noise and censors real exploration at once.

cards.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
cards.hook: GRPO dropped the value network from PPO and scored each answer against a group of sampled siblings — the cheap RL recipe that made DeepSeek-R1's reasoning trainable.

cards.title: Grading a Web App Feature by Feature, Then Sending the Reward Back to the Right Lines
cards.hook: A generated app fails in localized ways — a broken handler, a wrong selector. GRPO flattens all of it into one number. RCCA routes each rubric item's verdict back to the code that caused it.

cards.title: ZPPO: Put the Teacher in the Prompt, Not the Gradient
cards.hook: A small student learns from a bigger teacher without the drift that breaks on-policy RL - by feeding the teacher's answer into the prompt as a candidate to judge, never into the gradient.

cards.title: Is One Layer Enough? Training A Single Transformer Layer Can Match Full-Parameter RL Training
cards.hook: Full-parameter RL post-training updates every layer — but this study finds that training just ONE middle layer alone often recovers all the gains, and sometimes more.

cards.title: 100 GRPO Steps to Make a 350M Model Respect Your Schema
cards.hook: Small models are cheap but sloppy about output format. Three simple programmatic rewards and about 500 samples nearly doubled a 350M model's JSON pass rate.

cards.title: Training a Coding Model to Paint: RL Where the Reward Is How the Output Looks
cards.hook: The model writes JavaScript; the environment runs it in a headless browser, renders the painting, and scores the picture. A worked example of RL over an aesthetic, non-textual reward.

cards.title: When Real Speech Is Off-Limits, RL Beats Fine-Tuning on Synthetic Audio
cards.hook: Banks can't just collect real customer speech to adapt voice AI. Trained only on synthetic TTS audio, GRPO cuts word-error rate 40% more than supervised fine-tuning alone.

cards.title: Ring-Zero: Scaling Zero RL to a Trillion Parameters for Emergent Reasoning
cards.hook: Zero RL — reasoning trained on verifiable rewards, no human labels — had only been tried small-scale. At a trillion parameters, the model starts inventing reasoning habits nobody hand-coded.

cards.title: GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO Are Three Operations on One Number: The Group-Standard-Deviation Identity
cards.hook: GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO look like three separate fixes to reasoning RL — this paper proves they're just three settings of one dial: how much weight to put on a group's disagreement.

cards.title: Finding the Turn That Mattered in a Long Agent Rollout
cards.hook: RL with verifiable rewards scores a whole trajectory pass/fail, which tells an agent nothing about which of its forty turns was the pivotal one. AgentOPSD recovers turn-level credit without a critic.

cards.title: Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization
cards.hook: RLVR shapes rewards with entropy, but entropy can't tell useful uncertainty from confusion. CPO swaps in token-level disagreement — and shows on-policy distillation was a special case of it.

cards.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Direct On-Policy Distillation
cards.hook: RL post-training gets pricier as models scale, since it needs the strong model's own rollouts. Direct-OPD reuses a cheap RL run on a small model instead, transferring the direction RL moved it.

cards.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
cards.hook: A big model's softened probabilities say more than hard labels - they reveal how classes relate, so training a small model to mimic them transfers knowledge a one-hot target never could.

cards.title: One Symptom, Three Levers: A Critical Review of On-Policy Self-Distillation
cards.hook: Self-distillation drops the costly teacher by letting a model teach itself with privileged information. The asymmetry that creates the signal also biases it — into collapse.

cards.title: Quantization-Aware Healing: Distill, Don't Re-fit
cards.hook: Compress a 120B to 60B, drop it to 4 bits, and it breaks. QAT heals it slowly and then collapses; distilling from the original model instead gets there ~7x faster and stays stable.

cards.title: Quantization-Aware Distillation: Train the 4-bit Model, Don't Squash It
cards.hook: Liquid AI distilled BF16 teachers straight into Q4_0 students and recovered 97% of the accuracy that post-training quantization was throwing away.

cards.title: Distillation Without Training: Let a Strong Model Build the Weak One a Harness
cards.hook: A strong model writes the scaffolding — code, routing, format rules — and a weak model runs inside it. Average performance nearly doubled, 0.49 to 0.91, with no parameter updates at all.

cards.title: On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision
cards.hook: Self-distillation that finally deserves the name: no ground truth, no bigger teacher — just a model voting against itself and fixing where it was confidently wrong.

cards.title: DistilBERT: Smaller, Faster, Cheaper, Lighter
cards.hook: Distill during pre-training instead of after, and you get a general-purpose language model that is 40% smaller and 60% faster while keeping 97% of BERT's understanding.

cards.title: Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation
cards.hook: Distillation needs a teacher who knows more than the student. This paper gets that gap for free — not by informing the teacher, but by blinding the student.

cards.title: Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale
cards.hook: Distillation is expensive mostly for two boring reasons: the teacher hogs memory, and the KL loss materializes a huge vocab-by-sequence matrix. Fix both and a four-GPU job fits on one.

cards.title: Making Distillation Cheap: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss
cards.hook: You don't need the teacher in memory. Cache its top-K logits once, then train the student against the cache — same loss, ~29% faster per step, and 4x the context on one GPU.

cards.title: RecGPT-V3 Technical Report
cards.hook: Taobao's recommender now reasons about intent, not just click history. V3's trick: do that reasoning in compact latent tokens instead of long chain-of-thought, cutting output-token cost 200x at production scale.

cards.title: UI-MOPD: Teaching One GUI Agent Many Platforms Without Forgetting
cards.hook: Train a GUI agent on a new platform and it often forgets the old ones. UI-MOPD picks a different teacher per platform on the fly, so cross-platform learning stops fighting itself.

cards.title: Rethinking On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
cards.hook: Giving a model the answer as privileged context sounds like it should only help. For thinking models on long reasoning traces, it backfires — accuracy drops up to 17%, and this explains why.

cards.title: Nemotron-Labs-3-Puzzle-75B-A9B: Shrinking a 120B Model Without Retraining From Scratch
cards.hook: NVIDIA compressed its 120B-A12B Nemotron model down to 75B-A9B using 'Iterative Puzzle,' a post-training framework aimed at squeezing more inference efficiency out of an already-trained model.

cards.title: Distilling Across Different Tokenizers
cards.hook: On-policy distillation usually assumes teacher and student share a tokenizer. Map both into byte space and you can finally distil from a teacher whose vocabulary is nothing like yours.

cards.title: Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization
cards.hook: RLVR shapes rewards with entropy, but entropy can't tell useful uncertainty from confusion. CPO swaps in token-level disagreement — and shows on-policy distillation was a special case of it.

cards.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Direct On-Policy Distillation
cards.hook: RL post-training gets pricier as models scale, since it needs the strong model's own rollouts. Direct-OPD reuses a cheap RL run on a small model instead, transferring the direction RL moved it.

cards.title: Trust Region On-Policy Distillation
cards.hook: On-policy distillation breaks when teacher and student disagree too much. TrOPD only trusts the teacher where its supervision is reliable — and skips the rest.

cards.title: Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation
cards.hook: Every on-policy self-distillation method hand-picks what the teacher gets to see. LOPD makes that privileged context a learned vector instead of a design choice.

cards.title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
cards.hook: Instead of copying a teacher's raw outputs, this method distills only the *change* reasoning-tuning made — a sharper signal that beats standard on-policy distillation across math, science, and code.

cards.title: SEED: Self-Evolving On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
cards.hook: Outcome-only RL tells an agent whether an episode succeeded, not which step mattered. SEED has the policy mine its own trajectories for hindsight lessons, then distills them back in as dense, token-level signal.

cards.title: Denser ≠ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
cards.hook: On-policy self-distillation was supposed to fight forgetting in continual post-training — instead, denser self-distillation can drift further off course and collapse outright.

cards.title: OPID: On-Policy Skill Distillation for Agentic RL
cards.hook: Outcome-only RL tells an agent it failed but not which move was the mistake. OPID mines that lesson from the agent's own finished trajectories — turning hindsight into dense, per-token supervision.

cards.title: ZPPO: Put the Teacher in the Prompt, Not the Gradient
cards.hook: A small student learns from a bigger teacher without the drift that breaks on-policy RL - by feeding the teacher's answer into the prompt as a candidate to judge, never into the gradient.

cards.title: On the Geometry of On-Policy Distillation
cards.hook: On-policy distillation isn't a midpoint between fine-tuning and RL — it carves its own narrow path through parameter space, locking into a low-dimensional subspace early in training.

cards.title: Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation
cards.hook: Match the teacher's whole output sequence, not just word-by-word probabilities, and the student translation model can drop beam search while running about 10x faster.

cards.title: J-Zero: Co-Evolving a Challenger, a Solver, and a Judge From Zero Data
cards.hook: Self-improvement works when answers can be checked. J-Zero's trick for the unverifiable half: derive the judge's training labels from how each answer was produced, not from the judge's own scores.

cards.title: AgentMercury: Synthesizing Worlds, Not Tasks
cards.hook: Instead of building an environment per task, build a persistent business world with entities, services and invariants — and let the tasks fall out of it.

cards.title: Growing Agent Training Tasks by Recursion, at Five Cents Each
cards.hook: Hand-authored long-horizon agent tasks cost hundreds of dollars apiece. RST grows them recursively from verified seeds — 37,484 tasks at roughly $0.05 each, with no ceiling in sight.

cards.title: Skill Self-Play: Pushing the Frontier of LLM Capability with Co-Evolving Skills
cards.hook: Self-evolving models face a dilemma: verifiable environments are narrow, open-ended task generation is unreliable. This uses agent skills as the middle ground.

cards.title: Anchored Self-Play for Code Repair
cards.hook: Let a model train itself by writing bugs and fixing them, and you get a free difficulty curriculum — until it invents bugs no real codebase would produce. Anchored Self-Play keeps it honest.

cards.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning LMs with Self-Generated Instructions
cards.hook: Instead of paying humans to write instruction data, have the model write its own — bootstrap instructions, inputs, and outputs from its own generations, filter, and fine-tune.

cards.title: Textbooks Are All You Need (phi-1)
cards.hook: Train a 1.3B code model on a few billion tokens of 'textbook quality' data instead of raw web scale, and it scores 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval — data quality standing in for size.

cards.title: HOTFIXR: Targeted Synthetic Data for Multilingual Weaknesses
cards.hook: A model can answer the same question well in English and badly in Turkish. Rather than routing everything through English, probe the student's weak spots and synthesize data for exactly those.

cards.title: Trace: A Taxonomy-Guided Environment for Multidomain Visual Reasoning
cards.hook: Verifiable-reward training sharpened text reasoning but stalls on vision — exact-answer image tasks are hard to make at scale. Trace generates them procedurally, and it transfers to real benchmarks.

cards.title: FORT-Searcher: Shortcut-Resistant Tasks for Search Agents
cards.hook: Harder-looking questions aren't harder to search. FORT builds tasks where the intended search can't collapse into a cheap shortcut — and trains better deep-search agents on them.

cards.title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
cards.hook: Let the model write its own step-by-step rationales, keep only the ones that reach the right answer, fine-tune on those, and repeat — reasoning data that bootstraps itself.

cards.title: CLIP: Learning Visual Models from Language
cards.hook: Skip the fixed label list. Train on image–caption pairs so pictures and text share one space, and you can classify images from plain-text labels you make up on the spot.

cards.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (ViT)
cards.hook: Chop an image into patches, treat each like a word, and feed them to a plain Transformer. With enough pretraining data, it matches or beats convolutional networks.

cards.title: DALL·E 2 (unCLIP): Text-to-Image with CLIP Latents
cards.hook: Turn a prompt into a CLIP image embedding first, then diffusion-decode that embedding into a picture. A two-stage path from words to vivid, editable images.

cards.title: Segment Anything (SAM)
cards.hook: Click a point or drag a box, and it instantly masks the object — even in images it has never seen. SAM is a foundation model for segmentation.

cards.title: LingBot-Vision: Boundary-Aware Self-Supervised Pretraining
cards.hook: Masked-patch pretraining hopes boundary structure emerges on its own. This method forces the issue, masking exactly the regions a student can't infer by copying context — and beats a 7B model at 1.1B.

cards.title: ProxyPose: 6-DoF Pose Tracking via Video-to-Video Translation
cards.hook: Tracking a moving object's 3D pose normally needs a 3D model, depth, or masks. This method needs none of that — it translates video into a synthetic proxy, then solves the easy version of the problem.

cards.title: ReChannel: Repurposing Text-to-Image Diffusion for Dense Prediction
